Our findings highlight how statistical characteristics of specific problems influence the effectiveness and efficiency of different SDG variants, which have distinct reactions to varied noise levels and problem types. Building upon these discoveries, we develop an adaptive SDG method that dynamically adjusts learning rate and momenta based on batch statistics, significantly improving convergence across different noise scenarios and edge noise types. Notably, our proposed algorithm surpasses standardized best-practice methods, such as Momentum SGD, Adam, Ranger, and AdamW with large learning schedules.

Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading explanation for the strong-CP issue.  Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also arise in various modifications of the Standard Model, particularly in string theories.  Both axions and ALPs have compelling justifications as potential components of Dark Matter (DM), and substantial quantities would be generated at the sun's core.  For nearly two decades, the CAST experiment at CERN has been one of the primary efforts to detect axions.  The International Axion Observatory (IAXO) is an enhanced, large-scale version of axion-hunting technology, aimed at further refining searches for solar axions, achieving an elevated signal-to-background ratio of roughly 5 orders of magnitude.  

We now outline the astrophysical and experimental components of the search for solar axions in the context of the IAXO mission, specifically the astrophysical and experimental factors that will contribute to the astrophysical signal in the search process of the IAXO astrophysical signal, specifically the astrophysical signal of the IAXO search.  This involves detailed evaluations of the sun's core characteristics, including temperature, density, and helioseismic rotation rate.  We also examine ALP production, assuming the axions or ALPs are in a state of natural oscillation.  We review the x-ray bremsstrahlung background emitted by background

The possibility of developing several novel types of self-sustaining systems is suggested here, which could serve as innovative research tools and offer practical applications in the future. These potential systems have not been reported on an experimental basis earlier, to the best of our available knowledge. They are based on straightforward electrical circuits that can be used to illustrate and study fundamental dynamics at different stability thresholds. These circuits could also be easily adapted to display a wide variety of complex dynamics exhibited by similar, more complex systems in recent studies.

Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In comparison to other object manipulation techniques, dexterous grasping requires significantly fewer computational simulations due to its predictability. In contrast, other methods often rely on extensive simulations to match the accuracy of data generated by successful robotic experiments. Nevertheless, existing dexterous grasping datasets are limited, hindering the development of robots with skilled hands. In this research, we introduce DexGraspNet, a large-scale dataset designed to support the development of robots with dexterous hands across various applications. By leveraging Graspit! to conduct comprehensive simulations, our dataset includes precise descriptions of successful grasps and object poses for 1000 items categorized into 20 groups. Additionally, we develop GraspNet-DF, a novel technique that uses meta-learning to rapidly find effective dexterous grasps for unfamiliar objects, demonstrating superior performance and speed compared to other state-of-the-art methods. With the integration of a specially designed robotic setup called QuickChange, our research demonstrates that the grasps within our dataset are transferred seamlessly from simulations to real-world environments. The results and accompanying code are available online.

We developed a novel method to create motion-corrected, free-breathing 4D T2-weighted turbo spin echo MRI data using multi-model, model-order selection-based correction for respiratory fluctuation's periodic elements and diaphragm position data, which is more accurate than traditional amplitude-based correction and visually superior in image evaluation. This technique assessed the impact on T2-star relaxation on Escherichia coli bacteria and detected a 45% increase in relaxation rate under 300 MPa pressure. This method is compatible with most MRI systems and can be used for various applications.

A widely used knowledge extraction technique, knowledge distillation, fails to fully transfer internal representations from a strong model to a weak one because it takes an external view of the strong model's performance. To address this shortcoming, we introduce InDistill, a novel method that preserves the strong model's internal representations through self-supervised learning. By employing linear projections to mimic the strong model's features, InDistill achieves superior performance to traditional knowledge distillation, particularly on tasks with intricate data such as Point Cloud UNet.

Two smooth functions on the plane are classified as topologically equivalent if their graphs share a common perturbation, which results in graphs embedded in the plane via a smooth submersion. We prove that two linear-like functions can be topologically equivalent if and only if the foliations they induce on the plane are topologically equivalent, with each foliation being defined by the graph function. Moreover, our approach allows us to measure and track changes in these foliations as well as their respective linear-like submersions during perturbations. Our research explores the relationship between the topological equivalence of functions and the topological equivalence of their induced foliations, with particular emphasis on the case where each foliation is defined by a smooth submersion. We demonstrate that the conditions for each submersion being linear-like are not necessary for the result, which makes our finding more general. Our approach relies on the use of angular return maps and their properties, with the definition of angular return map corresponding to the concept of orientation return map proposed by J. Sotomayor in 1974, with modifications to accommodate non-orientable foliations.

Ecosystems that naturally thrive in dry environments have become increasingly vulnerable due to the rising risks of drought and the destructive powers of wildfires. To better understand and predict how these ecosystems are affected by a combination of local vegetation growth and the harmful effects of overgrazing, a theoretical model incorporating both spatial and temporal factors of plant growth and animal migration patterns needs to be developed. 

The model should take into account various factors, including the rate of plant growth, the conditions that plants require to survive, the frequency and duration of animal grazing, and the effects of overgrazing on the ecosystem. 

Research has shown that a class of mathematical models incorporating non-local interactions can effectively describe the dynamics of grazing systems and account for the long-distance movements of animals in search of food. 

Based on this understanding, a type of mathematical model that describes how plants and animals interact in a two-dimensional space can be applied to analyze the impact of overgrazing in ecological systems. 

This model consists of two interconnected equations representing the growth of plants and the migration of animals, with the animal movement influenced by a wide-ranging attraction to the plants covering the landscape. 

Mathematical analysis of this model reveals that it can experience a critical tipping point beyond which the ecosystem collapses under the intense pressure of overgrazing. 

This model can be applied to real-world scenarios by adjusting its parameters to match varying environmental conditions, such as different types of plant growth patterns and the extent to which animals travel in search of food.

A crucial tool called CountSketch is widely used for efficiently summarizing large datasets with a low storage requirement, offering an accurate representation of frequency information for large datasets. This simplicity and efficiency stem from its ability to sample and aggregate counts from fixed, uniformly-distributed vectors, regardless of the underlying data distribution. However, this simplicity is compromised when dealing with adversarial data distributions that significantly reduce the accuracy of Sketch summaries. Although the adaptability of these distributions is unknown, this research investigates a specific type of adversarial input: inputs that deliberately attempt to deceive or manipulate the accuracy of Sketch summaries. By developing new theoretical bounds for this specific scenario, this study enhances our comprehension of Sketch summary accuracy and informs the development of improved methods for creating these summaries. Specifically, this research presents a range of new theoretical bounds that demonstrate how the accuracy of Sketch summaries relates to specific data distribution characteristics, such as the summary's precision and the distribution's adaptability. By combining these findings, this study provides a more comprehensive analysis of Sketch summary accuracy and proposes a new theoretical limit for these summaries that applies to all adaptively chosen inputs. Interestingly, this research shows that CountSketch reaches this theoretical limit when the number of Sketch summaries approaches a specific threshold. This study also evaluates the accuracy of Sketch summaries on input datasets that are deliberately designed to adapt to the characteristics of the input data, and it compares these results to those of randomly chosen inputs. A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its application and performance across different hardware platforms. ipie shows significant advantages in usability, with a wide range of tunable parameters, and is capable of adapting to computational devices, ranging from multi-threaded CPUs to CUDA GPUs and Keras-based neural network processors. Moreover, ipie's performance can be enhanced by taking advantage of its ability to switch between recursion and cluster algorithms, and by using GPU acceleration and data parallelism. As a result, ipie's performance achieves notable improvements in terms of speed and accuracy on various benchmark molecules, outperforming existing AFQMC programs.

High-frequency trading could greatly benefit from a decentralized, transparent network, particularly one built with quantum technology that enables global connectivity and communication. The fundamentals of this trading system are similar to those of the quantum prisoner's dilemma, where immediate profits can lead to significant losses when other traders employ similar strategies, resulting in reduced earnings. The profitability of such trading depends on how effectively individuals can coordinate their actions with others, and technology rooted in quantum mechanics can facilitate healthy competition by allowing for the sharing of optimal decision-making models without manipulation or influence. The effectiveness of this trading system, therefore, relies on the security and privacy of the quantum network, and specifically, the ability to reliably manage two fundamental quantum mechanisms, decoherence and interference. The decay of a quantum state due to external influences can be leveraged to force traders to make concrete choices, and the ability to split a quantum particle while maintaining its coherence may hold the key to achieving the highest possible returns. The application of quantum mechanics to high-frequency trading has the potential to create a more equitable trading environment, and the development of related tools could pave the way for a variety of innovative uses.

This study investigates how to maximize the income generated from matching participants with their highest-valued counterparts, via an auction-style market where some of the participants can act as intermediaries, gaining benefits by facilitating matches between others. The market's structure is such that any participant can represent multiple others, and all agents truthfully report their exclusive willingness-to-pay values. We find that, even with these reports, determining optimal prices and values is inherently challenging when allowing multiple representatives, even in the case where there are only three participants. In contrast, we prove that, when every agent can represent themselves alone, determining these values becomes a relatively straightforward task. The complexity of the problem stems from the possible arrangements of representatives and their clients, leading to a need to analyze the market's dynamics across diverse scenarios. The findings indicate that, in general, maximizing the income generated is equivalent to ensuring that representatives prioritize their own interests through strategically chosen multi-round bidding processes, although this outcome does not necessarily align with the agents' individual interests. Specifically, we identify a situation in which maximizing the income generated is equivalent to achieving a state of equilibrium, where no agent would benefit from altering their strategic approach, unless all other agents were to alter their approach. To create abstractive summaries, current models still need significant perfecting of the instructions they're trained on. Yet, perfecting instructions manually is too labor-intensive for practical use. We suggest using planning to create customized prompts for improvement. In our study, we let a neural plan generator produce summary strategies for a transformer, and found that when the generator's parameters are learned during a brief optimization process, this planning approach can efficiently boost the quality of summaries produced by a pre-existing transformer, regardless of its architecture or training data volume. We tested our method with the Transformer-XL and BERT models, and saw it successfully create multiple relevant summary types. Furthermore, our prompts didn't need to be tailored for any specific dataset and were evaluated as being on par with expertly crafted prompts by human standards. Overall, our results suggest that neural prompt planning can be a viable strategy for perfecting the instructions given to language models.

This research paper presents necessary and sufficient conditions for a function with specific properties to have differentiability in higher dimensions. These conditions are derived by applying and combining previously established results from other studies. Key conclusions include:  If a given function, with certain specific attributes, is not differentiable at a particular point, then a new function, with similar properties, also fails to be differentiable at that same point. Conversely, if a function, with certain specific attributes, is differentiable at a particular point, then a new function, with similar properties, also may be differentiable at that point under specific mass distribution assumptions. Ultimately, this study yields differentiability theorems for higher-dimensional functions, which are inferred from previous one-dimensional results. Some examples are also provided to demonstrate the practical application of these theoretical findings.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, suggesting the need for more accurate entrainment measurement methods that can be applied to complex real-world situations, like normal conversations. To address this, we developed a new computational technique that identifies and analyzes the patterns of vocal synchronization in messy settings like natural conversations, allowing us to study entrainment in everyday social interactions. By comparing our method with established techniques, we found that it accurately detects vocal synchronization in both controlled and authentic environments. Furthermore, a study involving over 200 participants showed that our approach effectively captures essential aspects of entrainment without being overwhelmed by distracting factors like emotions or background noise. As a result, they achieved stronger connections in relationships, which didn't affect by emotional states or noise levels. This method opens up new possibilities for investigating entrainment in various contexts from a more holistic perspective.

This work delves into the mathematics behind quantum manipulation, focusing on operations within the unitary sphere, where objects are represented by vectors and transformations by linear maps with trace less than or equal to one. A crucial component of this study is the identification of suitable linear spheres, which are found to be essential for constructing a coherent model for quantum manipulation. By selecting the right form of linear spheres, a categorical model for quantum manipulation is established, which is then utilized to define categories for vectors and transformations. Furthermore, a lambda-S1 object is developed as a model for quantum information and classical data combination, which is found to exhibit properties of a closed symmetric monoidal category. This achievement enables the formulation of two equivalent modules for lambda-S1, which are found to possess distinct advantages: the trace module, which is closely related to the traditional quantum mechanics paradigm, and the unit trace module, which is analogous to the fundamental principle of unitary evolution. By establishing a model for quantum manipulation, a thorough understanding of quantum manipulation's structural attributes is gained, which are found to extend beyond the scope of monoidal categories for observables and effects.

This paper offers a theoretical analysis of two-dimensional electron systems, specifically in the context of the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE). We focus on energy spectra and wavefunctions for two quasiparticle excitations on the ground state within the composite Fermion (CF) FQHE, CF-2 quasiparticle, and electron-hole droplet (EHD) or hole-hole droplet (HHD) or their combinations. Building on Landau's gauge, we use a two-particle formalism to derive exact analytical solutions for the lowest modes of these systems. We also employ numerical calculations using many-body's Lagrangian and variational principle to determine the energy spectrum. These calculations yield precise results, validated by comparisons with established exact two-particle analytical solutions and quantum Monte Carlo methods, and both at zero and finite temperatures. Furthermore, this paper provides the complete analytical wavefunctions for these excitations, a first achievement in this area, allowing for an in-depth study of these states. We have also studied the properties of the FQHE's ground state by analyzing its two-particle form factor using both wavefunction and density approaches, resulting in precise analytical results that were previously inaccessible. These findings were also compared with numerical data obtained from density-matrix Monte Carlo method.

In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact between flowing ice and a rigid obstacle, a semicolective Stokes variational inequality is employed to describe stress, given that ice is cohesive but features discrete cracks. However, these cracks are not modelled, and instead, an edge element technique is used to approximate normal stresses on ice walls. Despite the absence of coercivity, a convergence theorem similar to those for semicoercive Stokes equations can be established, relying on Galerkin approximations of the variational inequality.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, researchers studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how its central star formation regulates its galactic outflows. The data revealed nearly one million solar masses being formed per year within its central region, along with a fifty million solar mass outflow rate. Despite the intense star formation, the outflow does not seem to be preventing further inflow of gas, likely due to a highly compressed gas disk acting as a buffer. Within its central region, carbon and oxygen material is being ejected at clump sizes of fifty thousand solar masses. The study found no evidence that the outflow is affecting the gas dynamics, instead it appears the gas is being fed to the central region to sustain the intense star formation. The findings support the concept of gas being fed to the central region to sustain the intense star formation. The study's data supports the idea of a pressure equilibrium between the gas in the central region and the gas being ejected.

Our research examined the connection between triangular flow and the direction of collision impact in gold and copper collisions at various energy levels using a multiphase transport model. Results showed that the triangular flow coefficient $v_3$ in central and peripheral collisions has a noticeable relationship with collision impact angle. This connection is more prominent at lower energy levels. Calculations also revealed that sound waves produced by quarks and gluons cause this correlation. Collaborative analysis of phenomena related to triangular and elliptical flow can help uncover properties of the collision system, such as its viscosity.

This research paper introduces a general robotic framework that can be applied across various simulation platforms, extending beyond physical robots in the real world. The key to achieving this is by utilizing high-level tasks, embedding these within a simulated environment that leverages the connection between simulation and reality. The authors then demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework through a practical demonstration of learning to pick and move objects with a robotic arm, all within the VirtualHome environment.

We investigate whether training convolutional neural networks on depth estimation instead of object classification enhances semantic segmentation. Despite depth estimation being a distinct task from semantic segmentation, we demonstrate that using a network already trained for depth estimation can improve semantic segmentation performance. However, this benefit is largely due to one specific aspect: the network having been trained on the network architecture itself, rather than actual depth data, which we refer to as "self-supervision from depth estimation". This concept is crucial because it allows us to show that similar improvements can be achieved by training on object detection, which is another task closely related to semantic segmentation. Therefore, we conclude that the main advantage comes from the network having been trained on a related task, not specifically depth estimation.

Let's consider the set of all analytic functions defined within the unit disk in the complex plane, along with those that have their values in the unit disk. We define a function g belonging to this set to be even if 1 - g(z) is symmetric about the real axis, and we define M and N to be the standard normalizators of g. We define a linear combination of g and its complex conjugate as a nonconstant, even log-harmonic function L, and define the K-L measure of L as the integral of the absolute value of L's n-th derivative over the unit disk, multiplied by n! plus the term involving the n-th derivative of the real part of L. We define R(L) as the infimum of the upper bounds for the K-L measure for all even, nonconstant log-harmonic functions L, where the upper bound is given by the expression (n + 1)(1 - n) norm of f, minus n, within the unit disk. In the case where n is a positive integer, we show that the infimum of the upper bound for the K-L measure for all even, nonconstant log-harmonic functions L, where the upper bound is given by the expression (n + 1)(1 - n) norm of f, minus n, is equal to (1 + n)/(1 + 2n) norm of f, minus n, and this result is achieved by considering specific even log

A new method for estimating Kendall's tau rank correlation coefficient in high-dimensional frameworks is developed. The proposed approach, comprising a two-stage process, first selects a subset of relevant features via cross-validated model selection, followed by an efficient computation of tau based on the subset. Building on the asymptotic results, two normalized versions of tau are studied and their limiting distributions are established, resulting in consistent tests for assessing correlations. The efficacy of the tests is demonstrated through simulations, which also compare their performance to those of alternative methods.

The proliferation of edge computing and AI-powered systems has led to a significant shift in how automotive networks function. From generating insights based on localized sensor data to enabling real-time AI-based control, these systems have become vital in creating intelligent connected mobility systems. Despite their importance, current solutions to edge computing in the automotive industry expose sensitive information to multiple entities, raising concerns about data security and privacy. This research proposes a novel, unified framework that safeguards confidentiality in automotive edge networks by utilizing distributed AI protocols. The framework relies on two primary mechanisms: locally optimized decentralized machine learning and device-based attribute-based encryption. This approach was demonstrated to provide enhanced confidentiality and privacy, and was tested in conjunction with a centralized decision-making system to ensure accurate insights and decision-making. The findings reveal that the framework maintains the accuracy of AI models at 98%, while keeping information privacy at 93%. This framework has the potential to create a highly secure and reliable foundation for emerging use cases in the automotive industry, such as AI-based vehicle control systems.

Euler characteristic is a topological invariant that compact manifolds cannot share. Therefore, given any finite list of integers, there exists a compact manifold whose Euler characteristic does not match any value in that list. This generalization of Minkowski's First Theorem has profound implications for the study of manifolds and their dimensions. The proof involves the intersection theory of compact manifolds and Borel's Freudenthal Domain theorem. Our work in this area is comprehensive and includes evidence that certain manifolds, such as Grassmannians, cannot be characterized by their cohomology rings. This is supported by the established Borel Freudenthal domain theorem and its implications for tubular neighborhoods of embedded submanifolds. The final outcome demonstrates that no compact manifold matches another in terms of their Euler characteristics, dimensions, and connected components.

A Holling-Tanner predator-prey model incorporating a strong Allee effect for both species is developed to simulate complex ecological interactions between predators and prey. The model incorporates predator saturation and a substantial increase in algae growth in the absence of predators, mirroring environmental restoration after predator colonization. The model's solutions are analyzed mathematically, and we demonstrate the long-term dynamics of this system by combining bifurcations and asymptotic phase space regions. The coexistence of predators and prey arises from the stability of a nonlinear limit cycle. Furthermore, we present examples of stable coexistence and show that the stable phase space area decreases as the model parameters increase.

The Facet Rotation Simplex method iteratively constructs a facially separate hyperplane in the feasible region by repeatedly rotating and projecting onto a fundamental circuit's facets, utilizing a direction derived from a maximal component-wise negative gradient direction. A key analysis reveals that each iteration direction is facially negative with respect to all previously constructed separate hyperplanes, while also demonstrating that the Facet Rotation Simplex method converges within n or k iterations, where n represents the problem's variable count and k the cone's dimension.

We are studying the NK1 ring, a specific type of double centralizer ring associated with a graded tuple of algebras. Building on Bak's unitary bimodule, we're looking into the NK1 ring of a particular type of graded tuple of algebras, including collections of matrix algebras, for various types of graded mappings.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Off-shell effects are found to hold considerable significance; their magnitude can reach up to 20% for the Wt channel and around 10% for the HT-dominated portion of the 2L2J+2J channel. A theoretical framework is also developed to estimate how these effects vary with the top quark off-shellness and jet energy and is successfully tested on a related calculation involving Higgs boson production via gluon fusion.

The susceptibility of deep neural networks to unknown and unexpected data has been a major area of interest in recent times. In particular, the field of pattern classification has been significantly impacted by this issue, and it's most pronounced in the area of anti-spoofing, where a significant challenge exists in the absence of accurate predictions when encountering unfamiliar templates or classes during inference. Zero-shot face anti-spoofing involves detecting anti-spoofing signals without manual template labeling, utilizing the inherent semantic structure information embedded in the data's embedding space. A promising technique known as transformers has been utilized effectively in the creation of successful anti-spoofing models that operate on raw data. We investigate whether using a vision transformer dedicated to understanding complex and challenging data can outperform its pre-trained counterpart on zero-shot anti-spoofing tasks. To this end, a novel anti-spoofing model utilizing a dedicated vision transformer was developed and tested, replete with essential features and mechanisms that enhance its anti-spoofing capabilities and overall flexibility. Experiments conducted on the CALFW, LIVES, MORPH-2, SiW-M, and SiW-I datasets show that our proposed model consistently achieves superior performance relative to generic transformers and state-of-the-art anti-spoofing methods on zero-shot and semi-supervised tasks. Moreover, our findings indicate that utilizing a dedicated vision transformer leads to significant performance gains, ranging from 4.12% to 6.88% in zero-shot

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive field remains elusive. Nevertheless, considerable progress has been made in recent times across multiple performance metrics. Our environmental mapping project utilizing deep reinforcement learning further contributes to this trajectory. Our paper explores the possibilities and pitfalls of deep reinforcement learning for autonomous vehicles and presents critical environmental hurdles for potential resolution. A comprehensive review of current deep reinforcement learning algorithms and suggested remedies for these challenges is provided, accompanied by a demonstration of our self-driving system and an examination of its effectiveness in addressing these issues.

Evolutionary algorithms are widely used to tackle complex optimization issues, particularly in areas where other solutions may not be effective. When using parallel computing for these problems, an issue known as evaluation time bias often arises due to the greater expense of evaluating certain solutions compared to others. This can lead to a disproportionate focus on those populations with more slowly evaluated members, often resulting in the premature termination of the overall optimization process. This paper explores a novel parent selection technique to mitigate the effects of evaluation time bias in multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. Our approach ensures that, when making selections, the algorithm considers both the solutions' qualities and the evaluation time of their respective populations, using a proportional representation technique to achieve a well-balanced diversity. Our findings, which emerged from running a comprehensive set of experiments on multi-objective optimization problems, demonstrate that the proposed technique is effective in reducing the impact of evaluation time bias and, as a consequence, often enhances the quality of obtained results. This innovative parent selection technique has been included in its original form in the NEHGA 2 algorithm, a multi-objective non-linear evolutionary algorithm.

The large sample size of gravitational wave standard stars and the numerous microlensing planets found recently, indicate that future large ensemble studies of gravitational wave standard stars using Extremely Large Telescopes will undoubtedly result in identifying numerous planetary systems similar to OGLE-2017-BLG-1434L, a planet bound to a low-mass star whose presence was initially detected through a strong microlensing effect. To verify the cold temperature of the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 planet, a detailed spectral analysis using the P1640 mask subarray was conducted at 1.4 to 1.05 micrometers. This analysis, combining the parallax method with the spectrum analysis, confirmed that OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 has an effective temperature of around 2600 Kelvin and a mass of approximately 0.07 solar masses. As a result, the planet has a larger mass than 90% of ultra-cold dwarf planets discovered so far, which, based on current knowledge, makes it a challenging target for direct imaging technology to detect the planet directly with ELTs.

We derive a high-frequency expansion of the time-oscillating Lindblad generator. This finding allows us to analyze the long-time behavior of open quantum dynamics described by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and a time-dependent dissipation term. Initially, we establish a high-frequency expansion for the dissipation operator and then use it to develop an expansion for the dissipation flow. Our research also addresses precessing coherent dynamics and reveals that, despite the system's unitary time evolution, a term proportional to the Hamiltonian's commutator with the dissipation operator appears in the expansion. This term reflects an equilibrium shift that occurs as time evolves.

Our recent studies of the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reveal the emergence of magnetic irreversibilities and spin freezing in the vicinity of the first-order phase transition between magnetic and non-magnetic order at x ≈ 0.4. Neutron scattering measurements also indicate a decrease in order caused by spin freezing, which complements the coexistence of ferromagnetism and spin freezing observed in the same system using small-angle neutron scattering. This suggests that both the ordered and disordered phases in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ exhibit magnetic behavior.

Our research involves the analysis of HI observations from the Galactic Ring Survey, which reveal a 1.3 km/s line in the direction of the star-forming region G176.51+00.20. This enigmatic line cannot be attributed to cosmic velocity dispersion or a diffuse molecular cloud. Two possibilities are explored to explain this line, which may be related to the region's strong ionized gas cloud. Firstly, radiative amplification through a process other than stellar radiation, or secondly, a gas shell moving at approximately 6 km/s per second. Both scenarios are supported by existing data in the area.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a gap that meets specific criteria, and a particular class of greedy beta-transformations with a gap that serves as an example for a class of non-topologically equivalent systems.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly CP-odd final states (J/\psi pi^+ rho^-) in 1 fb^-1 of pp collision data at 7 TeV, collected with the LHCb detector, researchers computed the phi_s value. After incorporating this information along with results from another experiment (J/\psi pi^-), the combined value for phi_s is approximately 64.42 +/- 11.94 degrees with a confidence interval of 68.2%, in line with the standard model's predicted value.

Deep neural networks have achieved groundbreaking results in image classification tasks; however, their performance often suffers when applied to images sourced from different areas. In this research, we investigate and compare various approaches to adapting neural networks for image classification tasks in distinct environments. Firstly, we examined and differentiated between three primary strategies: shifting labels, adjusting models, and merging data sets. Subsequently, we evaluated a range of established methods, including self-supervised pre-training, active learning, transfer learning, cross-view training, streamlining networks, and others. These approaches were tested on the ImageNet dataset, with preliminary experiments showing that a streamlined ResNet model demonstrated exceptional resistance to environment changes. Moreover, the adapted methods were tested on environmental benchmarks such as DomainNet, VOC11-SUN, and CUB, revealing that a combination of pre-training and streamlining techniques yielded the most effective adaptations. The source code for our research has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ash123sys/Deep_Network_Domain_Adaptation.

Let $q$ be a power of a prime $p$, and consider the ring $p$-adics as well as the field $p$ over which $q$ is raised. A previous study, focusing on counting curves in $\mathbb F_q^2$, was conducted by D. Ginzburg who established a generating function for this counting curve problem. Building upon his work, the present research expands on that study by investigating the counting curve problem in the context of $\mathbb F_q^2$ with an emphasis on the role of residual characteristics. As a result, the paper derives an updated formula for the generating function specific to characteristics 2 and establishes a new conjecture for characteristics 3 and above, all in characterizing the counting curve problem in $\mathbb F_q^2$.
A visual proof shows that there are exactly 240 triangles in a tetrahedral grid, consisting of four overlapping tetrahedra, by counting them as 240 distinct triplets.

Graph Neural Networks have achieved remarkable success in tackling a variety of graph-based learning challenges. A major consideration in designing these models is selecting an appropriate mixing strategy for distinct graph nodes. There has been a lack of methodology to systematically vary the mixing approach, leaving a significant gap in the model development process. In our investigation, we present a novel parameterized GNN model called PhGNN, where the mixing parameter allows for a gradual transition between conventional GNN models and convolutional neural networks. To achieve this, we introduce a parameterized filter transformation, enabling the model to be differentiable and extensible. Notably, PhGNN extends the capability of conventional GNNs to process symmetric random fields and special cases like MGNN, while also outperforming existing models on standard metrics. Our findings particularly show that PhGNN is beneficial for node classification tasks.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To investigate its development, we analyzed the galaxy system's substructure. Using the $m_{500}$ and $\sigma_{500}$ parameters based on X-ray data, we found the system exhibits substructure with a ratio $C_{500}/C_{0.5}$ being 0.86 for a cool core and 0.74 for a disrupted core. Its $f_{h,500}$ fraction falls at 0.47, indicating a high presence of radio halos. By choosing two temperature pairs from (1.70, 1.74) or (1.74, 1.76) keV, we calculated the system's asymmetry in terms of density and temperature. Regardless, the system appears to possess a two-phase accretion nature. Its spatial distribution of the two-phase medium matches the system's substructure characteristics. Interestingly, the upper bound of its radio halo age is 0.73 Gyr, implying that the halo likely formed during the system's initial stages.

The training of neural networks utilizing the Legendre Memory Unit, a component within the Emergent Lorentzian Neural Network, is notoriously unresponsive to adjustments in the learning rate due to its intrinsic properties. The reason behind this challenge can be traced to the network's nonlinear transformation within the LMU layer, which significantly varies depending on the initial state. Consequently, a conventional training approach proves ineffective in this context. To overcome this limitation, researchers have devised a novel adaptation of the generalized YOLO method, tailored specifically for the LMU layer, and demonstrated that this modified approach yields superior outcomes when combined with mixed initialization techniques. Moreover, experiments conducted with both single-graphical-unit and multi-graphical-unit networks showed that the LMU layer can be efficiently trained in parallel, thus facilitating parallelization without compromising the underlying theory.

As the 21st century's initial decades come to a close, it becomes increasingly evident that the fundamental theory of particle physics, the Standard Model, is nearing its threshold of completion. Nevertheless, a significant barrier to fully resolving it has been a set of "light, fast-moving, weak-interacting particles," commonly referred to as WIMP-null particles. These particles elude detection by the large underground laboratories where such particles are typically sought. A new generation of experimental endeavors is being formed to design methods for detecting these particles across a broader spectrum than before. This paper provides an overview of the underlying scientific issues, discusses initial observations from studies conducted decades ago as well as the current and planned endeavors to investigate these particles.

We conducted an investigation into the dynamic process of developing a language through a simulation of the 'Naming Game' when agents are mobile and can migrate. In this scenario, each agent is associated with a specific region, and its language development is influenced by both the local environment and neighboring areas. As a result of exchanging names with fellow agents, the language evolves toward a uniform, consistent platform. Moreover, our findings indicate that the ultimate language is determined by large-scale networks and that the rate of name exchange within these networks directly correlates with the size of the corresponding clusters. Interestingly, our analysis also reveals that the time it takes for the language to converge is inversely related to the size of these networks.

Momentum-based methods in physics-informed neural networks significantly boost training efficiency by stabilizing the network deep within the optimization process, particularly during the late stages of training. This is accomplished through momentum's ability to prevent coefficient overshooting and accurately capturing high-order differential equations while minimizing the impact of spectral bias. By leveraging momentum, PINN training becomes more directed and less influenced by the network's spectral characteristics, resulting in better convergence. This improved performance is showcased through momentum-based training of a PINN model that accurately models and predicts the solution to the heat equation.

We examine a combined system of wave equations, one driven damped and the other purely elastic, connected through a boundary interface with damped behavior. The damped wave is subject to Kelvin-Voigt damping limited to the interface, creating discontinuities in the related diffusion equation. The damped and undamped waves interact at the interface via normal traction and the damped wave is additionally influenced by external forces. We provide exact estimates of energy decay for the damped wave's displacement and the undamped wave's velocity within the damped domain. We extend these decay rates to the damped wave's velocity using a classical approach from Helmeras' work on stability analysis.

Reinforcement learning in complex environments with multiple linked tasks poses a significant problem, leading to a large issue with finding efficient solutions. This research explores a new approach to tackle this challenge, drawing inspiration from algebraic geometry concepts. The team introduced a model-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that initially uses a high-level abstract representation of tasks to split the problem into manageable sub-components and learn their connections. Following this, they employ Inductive Logic Programming to frame and resolve lower-level tasks within a logical framework, making the system easier to understand for humans. The proposed framework is tested on a simplified scenario from the real-world, achieving better results compared to traditional approaches.

We investigate how quantum squeezing affects the optical asymmetry in a twin-laser system that uses a nonlinear crystal to interact via spatial mode coupling.  The optical asymmetry is represented by an asymmetry operator defined as the difference between the real-field amplitudes in two directions. We examine how non-degenerate beam parameters and spatial mode structures influence optical asymmetry when the laser system operates at its steady state. Specifically, we look at how the sidebands of the field shift in response to different parameters. We demonstrate that the optical asymmetry can be controlled by varying the ratio of carrier power to sideband power as well as the phase and ratio of pump power to nonlinear crystal length.  Notably, we find that the optical asymmetry shows non-reciprocity when the pump power ratio changes, even in a system designed to be symmetric.  Additionally, quantum squeezing in one direction enhances the optical asymmetry while squeezing in the other direction reduces it.  To further understand the behavior of this system, we have made a phenomenological analysis based on the physical processes involved in mode coupling.  Our results indicate that the optical asymmetry can be manipulated by non-classical means in a twin-laser system that interacts through spatial mode coupling, which has the potential to be applied in quantum optics and photonics research.

This research investigates functional properties that remain unchanged even after translating them by a given amount. Our focus lies on the highest degree possible for this translation invariance. This corresponds to a well-studied topic that has been explored by numerous researchers, including Fenton type minimax problems. The goal of our work is to examine the properties of summation functions that have been translated. We will define and establish the concepts of monotonicity, alternating monotonicity, type Fenton, and study their behavior in minimax problems, as well as provide sample calculations to illustrate these concepts.

Li-$6$ FET detectors can detect dark matter at prices lower than conventional detectors, additionally allowing for the Li-$6$ atom's Li I $2\cdot 1$ state's properties to be studied in high vertical magnitudes, thus making it an ideal substance for analyzing the dark matter's dependence on spin. Research will focus on the Li-$6$'s spin-dependent interactions in high vertical magnitudes through shadow material interactions - a concept where Li-$6$ interacts with a substance more sensitive to spin than regular dark matter interactions. By applying the PAW model on the Li-$6$'s $2\cdot 1$ state, the formula for the interaction cross-section is established. By examining the Li-$6$'s spin-dependent interactions under various conditions, the interaction cross-section can be determined in different ways. The experiment will involve the Li-$6$'s interaction cross-section being measured at 100 eV/$\text{pb}$ - a figure that surpasses current limits by two orders of magnitude, thus demonstrating a novel approach to study the Li-$6$'s properties and the interaction between spin-dependent dark matter and matter.

This research presents a novel approach to the common image restoration tasks of denoising, deblurring, and deringing. We frame these tasks within the context of estimating an image's underlying kernel that has been distorted in some way. Previous studies proposed modeling the kernel's shape using Gaussian kernels, which were optimized via maximum likelihood. However, the practicality of this approach was compromised by its poor capacity in model capacity-expansion and the difficulty in solving the related optimization problem. To this end, we introduce the Kernel Mixture model, which treats the kernel as a combination of pre-trained base kernels. Experiments show that our approach can efficiently expand model capacity and achieve significant improvements in processing larger images, datasets, and multiple degradation types simultaneously.

This paper introduces a new concept called uniform and nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations along with their co-algebra versions, building upon earlier work by Kauffman, Banach-Alchurs-Przybyszewski, and Dargham. It showcases how these equations link solid tangle theories in topology and quantum invariants in low-dimensional topology. A significant finding reveals that uniform and nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations are equivalent when applied to algebras with identical structure constants, a property known as the homogeneous algebra condition. This research culminates by proposing a number of open questions for further exploration.

Hoare logic offers a straightforward, widely accepted approach to formally specifying and verifying the consequences of programs using first-order logic. Nonetheless, its rigorous mathematical nature makes it impractical for specifying algorithms in a natural language context. To bridge this gap, we present a practical verification method that translates Hoare logic into a form that can be applied to compiled programs. We use an extended version of first-order logic that incorporates explicit modality and structure conventions to represent the overall program structure, thereby facilitating a more efficient separation of concerns between logical expressions and program code. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply it to a simple sorting algorithm and demonstrate its ability to formally establish the algorithm's correctness based on a natural language description.

Distributed consensus is a foundational concern for distributed systems, with significant financial losses resulting from inadequate consensus operations in areas such as stock trading. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages a shared register across up to $t$ faulty or malicious processes with only $f$ dominant processes, where $f$ is less than a third of the total number of processes. The existing Canopus design fails to account for faults and malicious processes, resulting in a non-terminating state when a failure or malicious behavior occurs.

Despite the widespread use of unilamellar vesicles in research, there's a lack of reliable methods to measure the flexural modulus or bending rigidity of lipid bilayers. The phase shift technique, commonly employed to assess the size and charge of liposomes, also has the potential to be used for moduli measurement, as it's sensitive to changes in swelling pressure. The technique works by exposing the liposomes to an alternating electric field in a buffer solution, thereby detecting changes in reflectivity when the liposomes start to swell. Our study focuses on measuring the effect of cholesterol on the swelling behavior of lipid bilayers, using the phase shift method in conjunction with zeta potential measurements. The results suggest that while adding cholesterol increases the swelling resistance of lipid bilayers, it also reveals the presence of a specific length scale in the system, specifically the lipid molecule spacing. This observation implies that the swelling process occurs through a mechanism involving the disruption of lipid molecules rather than a random lipid addition. Moreover, our study offers a novel approach to estimate the moduli of lipid bilayers using the phase shift method, as it enables the direct determination of the mechanical properties of unilamellar vesicles.

The article examines the fundamental properties of a star, born from a quantum bounce occurring in the two-dimensional de Sitter spacetime generated by loop quantum gravity. This star's structure is analogous to a 2D de Sitter pseudosphere, with its own version of the de Sitter circle, where the quantum bounce is the origin and where three-dimensional de Sitter spacetime emerges from this origin. This paper reinterprets previous research, revealing that the model developed earlier, based on an isotropic model, is a portion of a larger picture and a consequence of considering the complete spacetime. Additionally, this study demonstrates that the model's initial conditions can be adjusted by manipulating the ADM Hamiltonian's constraints. This research also confirms that the model's initial stages are governed by potential-dominated dynamics. This paper further establishes that, in the later stages of the star's life, the spacetime metric behaves as expected for a radiative atmosphere, consistent with Eddington's vacuum boundary conditions, and that the star's size exhibits a power-law growth pattern, similar to that described by Poincaré's model for madelung's prescription in LQG.

Over the course of Phase I, which lasted from 2003 to2017, the Pierre Auger Observatory collected comprehensive astrophysical data on ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, including 61 events with energies surpassing 50 EeV and 9 particles exceeding 80 EeV.  In the same period, data on 19 high-energy neutrinos was also gathered, with eight exceeding the energy threshold of 60 EeV.  This paper details the precision with which the experiment accurately measured the arrival locations, depths in the atmosphere, and energy of these powerful particles, as well as whether their arrival patterns exhibit anisotropy and multiplicity.

Incorporating deep neural networks into high-level computer vision tasks has a significant history dating back to the late 1990s, however recent advancements in detection, segmentation, and tracking using deep networks have mainly built upon further development of convolutional networks. We contend that a significant issue in deep object detectors is the lack of uncertainty modeling, and therefore propose BayesOD, a pioneering approach that utilizes Bayesian inference to accurately estimate uncertainty in object detection tasks. By training a network to represent the variational approximation posterior as a two-stream CNN, BayesOD is able to acquire reliable uncertainty metrics for detection and classification. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art confidence metrics, and shows potential for future applications in various tasks.

Recent advances in Cognitive Traffic Systems have highlighted the significance of integrating traffic analytics and traffic control, leveraging the power of the Internet of Things and Operational Intelligence. Traffic analytics plays a crucial role in improving the effectiveness of traffic management by providing insights into the present state of traffic. One potentially promising approach to traffic analysis is visual recognition of changing traffic patterns, or traffic bubbles. These ephemeral scenes, captured by in-vehicle cameras, can be used to predict incidents like red lights and accidents, thereby enabling more intelligent traffic management systems. However, recognizing these scenes remains an intricate task due to the distinct characteristics of traffic bubbles and limited labeled data availability. We address this challenge by formulating a Red Light Prediction model based on traffic bubbles, using Snippet Synthesis Snippets, a novel approach that combines Snippet Synthesis with supervised learning. We test and validate this model, achieving the highest accuracy to date on the Red Light 4K Dataset without additional manually labeled images.

In categories without gray categories or biproducts, we use two methods to find substitutions that can potentially coerce $A \to B$ into $F(f)$, and we link these methods to coherence conditions, and show they are equivalent to the existence of biproducts, at least in gray categories. These methods involve reevaluating gray boxes and gray polygons, and specifically, we utilize the concepts of double categories, bialgebras, and bi-modules to facilitate this reevaluation. Additionally, we utilize the framework of lax functors to create a diagram that represents these gray structures as a specific type of commutative diagram, and this framework allows us to make further conclusions about the coherence conditions in gray categories.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on brain MRI is an essential element in various neurological research applications. Current deep learning techniques primarily focus on a single type of hippocampal segmentation, despite the benefits of combining multiple datasets for more comprehensive research. This study contributes a novel, unified approach that combines multiple convolutional neural networks for hippocampampal segmentation, specifically tackling challenges presented by Alzheimer’s disease and epilepsy. This framework consists of a unified backend system, allowing the use of shared hippocampal features to accommodate the differences in hippocampal appearance resulting from Alzheimer’s and epilepsy. Preliminary experiments were conducted on the automatic hippocampal segmentation challenge dataset provided by International Hippocampal Study in Hippocampal Study in Hippocampal Study (2017), along with the epilepsy dataset from Kirby Institute, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia. Analytical comparison was made with respected state-of-the-art techniques, including 3D U-Net and U-Net. The findings indicate a significant enhancement both in terms of computation efficiency and segmentation accuracy. This study is a first in utilizing multiple convolutional neural networks for hippocampal segmentation in both Alzheimer’s and epilepsy applications.

We investigated a peculiar phenomenon in coherent mode conversion within waveguides, where an initial hole would be absent in its mode pattern. To explain this occurrence, we utilized the concept of transversal modes and discovered that each mode is either entirely absorbed in the waveguide or has zero projection onto the hole. Upon further reflection, we realized that this phenomenon can be seen as a form of entanglement between horizontal and vertical modes, resulting from the waveguide's unique properties. We found that when the waveguide's dimensions are carefully chosen, the waveguide can serve as an entanglement generator under specific conditions.

Our research identifies the Chandra X-ray Observatory's capabilities in studying cosmic rays at low Earth orbit by utilizing data collected by the instrument. This involves detecting particles trapped in the upper atmosphere, which are then broken down into hydrogen nuclei. Our findings are based on a in-depth analysis by creating a 3D probability map of the near-Earth hydrogen nuclear density from simulated data collected over a full solar cycle. By comparing the model with observational data and taking into account variations in solar activity, we found that the trapped particles primarily consist of a rotating barotropic jet accompanied by long-term spatial variations in the upper atmosphere. These phenomena are more pronounced during active solar periods. Furthermore, we discovered that the trapped particle population changes direction at geomagnetic poles and alters depending on different magnetic latitude zones. Our research highlights the effectiveness of the Monte Carlo method in understanding nutritional patterns of cosmic rays in the Earth's environment, which can be applied to other space missions.

A comprehensive neural network structure for Deep Graph Neural Networks (D-GNNs) is
proposed, capitalizing on the dynamic coevolution of skeleton simplification and edge
rewiring. The 'Global Pyramid-like Shrinkage Skeleton' technique streamlines node
connections through hierarchical hierarchical hierarchical hierarchical hierarchical
pyramidal structures, incorporating multi-level skeletal elements. These elements
contribute to learning hierarchical node representations, with the 'Local Topology Link
Rewiring' approach altering edge connections to concentrate on neighborhood relationships.
D-GNNs' performance is evaluated on various chemical data sets, yielding superior
results compared to current state-of-the-art models.

To protect user privacy while reconstructing a missing part of a low-rank matrix based on observed samples, several private matrix completion methods have been developed. Existing solutions either guarantee precise recovery when a sufficient number of samples is available or provide a confidentially guaranteed accuracy level. Our method achieves the first private matrix completion results with geometric convergence, while ensuring the accuracy gap holds without samples for certain types of matrices. Furthermore, for the standard case where samples come from a random subspace of the matrix, the proposed approach features the narrowest known gaps between privacy and accuracy. This new approach is also statistically secure, as it is not influenced by the random sampling process. Our analysis relies on a novel application of the Huber method, and we also present a new efficient algorithm using generalized methods for solving matrix factorization. Both of these techniques could be useful in other matrix completion tasks that are not private.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, separate from PAHs. In this framework, a subset of interstellar PAHs is being real-time refined to align with new data across various fields. New models for the polarization properties of grains, as well as type-2 polarization, have been introduced. Results demonstrate a substantial alignment between the proposed model and observed polarization patterns. Additionally, this model successfully replicates the general forms of the four primary spectral energy distribution components, which are primarily attributed to grain emission. It does this by emitting light at frequencies proportional to 1/λ (similar to black bodies) and exhibiting polarization properties dependent on the orientation of larger grains. Also, this model replicates many properties of PAH features by accurately modelling their response to environmental conditions. In line with the concept of "global chemistry", a set of chemical reactions has been developed to describe the origin and decay of specific PAHs. As such, this model is applied uniformly to all four components of dust in the interstellar medium, which are collectively referred to as "Astrodust". In addition to its practical applications, this model provides a narrative that describes the natural world at a level of abstraction.

The research on exoplanets, especially those around small stars, is still relatively underdeveloped, but studying these planets around low-mass stars can provide valuable insights into how planets form and interact with their surrounding disk material. This study used data from the Spitzer Space Telescope as part of its Legacy of Exoplanets to study low-mass star systems, including the 1.2 solar mass star CIDA 1, which revealed a 140 millarad asymmetry in its disk. This asymmetry is consistent with a 10 Jupiter mass planet located at 0.2 astronomical units from the star. Analyzing the SPECTRE data found that the CIDA 1 disk has transitioned from an accretion to an erosion phase within the past 5 million years, which is consistent with the presence of a massive planet as suggested by the photometric data. This study also detected similar asymmetry and evidence of disk erosion around another low-mass star system, VHS 8, which supports its similarity to CIDA 1 in terms of mass and radial asymmetry, however, no reliable mass measurement could be provided for the VHS 8 planet.

The Lights Out problem on a graph involves determining tap sequences that can switch off all the vertices. A key property is that the problem is solvable if a given graph has no biconnected components. However, the simplicity of this condition does not translate to a straightforward solution algorithm, as demonstrated by its association with the NP-hard Tap Cover problem. In this research, a tap sequence with the maximum number of activations is identified as the'most taps problem' and is shown to be NP-hard even for simple graph structures. A polynomial-time solvable variant, the least taps problem, is also introduced, but the original problem is shown to be hard even when limited to specific graph configurations, such as graphs with relatively low codegree or those that are induced Ramsey for small sizes.

This study presents a novel, advanced image segmentation technique that combines a cutting-edge image restoration model, resulting in a state-of-the-art segmentation approach. The conventional Mumford-Shah image segmentation model is extended through the incorporation of total variation regularization, enabling robust segmentation of images with minor disturbances and imperfections. The resulting model offers superior segmentation performance, particularly for images with edges to a limited number of non-zero elements. To efficiently solve this problem, an optimized computational algorithm is established. The method initiates with a fast first-order gradient descent for a simplified version of the model. Subsequently, it employs alternating minimization to solve the optimization problem, with the minimization problem being addressed through a first-order gradient descent and an approximate solution being sought for the maximization problem. The level set function is explicitly defined in the model's partial variational formulation, allowing for simultaneous optimization. The outcome of this method is evaluated using multiple benchmark images, yielding exceptional results.

Over the past 30 years, Abstract Interpretation has served as a primary paradigm for sound over-approximation in a diverse array of computer science applications. This methodology uses abstract domains to simulate the complex behavior of programs, controlling abstraction with precision via chosen domains and Galois connections. Although standard AB tools have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of computer science disciplines, they have historically suffered from one fundamental flaw: either analyzing programs with transient bugs or failing to terminate on programs with them. This is because traditional AB domains are inherently monotonic, forcing tools to continually tighten their analysis until they eventually become unable to make any further improvements, leading to models that reflect all potentially reachable states and result in false positives on programs containing disallowed behaviors. In order to overcome this limitation, we suggest introducing non-monotonic abstract domains that temporarily relax analysis constraints during an test or, alternatively, static and dynamic analysis combinations that take advantage of their respective strengths.

We investigate the topological phonons in oxide perovskites by focusing on the spin phonon coupling, which is caused by the interaction between the spin of a central atom and the surrounding ions' vibrations. Our study reveals that the spin phonon coupling can be described by a simplified model involving a central atom's spin and a 2D vibrational lattice. This interaction adjusts the vibrational modes' characteristics and creates a new topological phase transition in the system. Unlike other topological phonon systems, the spin phonon coupling is successful in numerous materials across different groups of oxide perovskites due to its diversity of structural conditions. Furthermore, the spin phonon coupling enables the induction of a significant phonon Hall conductivity and massive anomalous phonon Hall effect even in bulk materials, and it also shows resilience under external magnetic fields. Finally, we demonstrate that the spin phonon coupling can be easily controlled and modulated by exciting the central atom's spin through light irradiation under experimental accessibility, thereby opening up the possibility of using light to create and regulate topological phonons in bulk materials.

Identifying proper algorithmic processing orders is crucial for efficiently detecting deviations from data normality and minimizing the impact of such anomalies in clustering tasks. This process necessitates the determination of algorithmic processing orders to prioritize the most critical data items until a convergence criterion is met. A new approach has been developed for outlier detection in clustering tasks, relying on a metric space graph without any specific network characteristics. This graph-based method enables the detection of anomalies in metric spaces and facilitates the determination of the most critical data items for processing. The approach also introduces a new decision criterion for evaluating processing efficiency, and it has been further extended by implementing a metric for measuring data similarity within the metric space. This results in a novel outlier detection method and facilitates the development of efficient clustering solutions. To validate this new approach, the performance of the method has been tested with real-world datasets from diverse domains, and it has been further analyzed for its scalability and adaptability to different metric spaces. This evaluation includes a range of metrics such as runtime, distance distribution, and clustering performance.

Our research explores an atomic model that oscillates between two potential energies and faces a mirror with a finite width. The atomic model considers both electric coupling with the mirror and magnetic influence from an external magnetic field. Under these conditions, the atomic excitation leads to the emission of radiation, which follows a specific black-body radiation thermal spectrum, and this thermal effect can be overridden by resonating the atom at a specific frequency by adjusting its velocity or the magnetic field strength, thereby satisfying energy conservation through radiation recoil. This phenomenon of stimulated emission by overriding energy constraints has the same underlying principles as lasers but occurs due to a different mechanism of atomic excitation.

Graph representation learning has garnered significant interest, but the existing approaches often overlook a crucial factor - ensuring that the learned representations preserve community structures that are in line with the real-world standards of fairness. Consequently, there is a need for a more refined understanding of graph representation learning, specifically one that addresses and accounts for the presence of diverse communities. 

We propose the concept of localized community fairness, which involves adjusting node embeddings (such as node2vec) by prioritizing neighborhoods that adhere to fair standards. To achieve this, we utilize a fairness-sensitive distance metric that combines the traditional Wasserstein distance with a customized variant, tailored to accommodate the complex requirements of localized fairness. The key innovations of our approach involve (i) defining the concept of localized fairness and its applicable scenarios, (ii) developing a suitable metric for measuring fairness that accounts for both global and neighborhood differences, and (iii) demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive theoretical analysis and real-world testing. 

Based on this novel principle of localized fairness, we develop a novel graph learning model that effectively captures the intricate details of node connections and is capable of performing accurately in fairness-related tasks. To further optimize our model, we integrate it with an innovative reweighting technique, which enables us to tackle the challenge of unequal node counts by assigning higher importance to nodes that represent pivotal communities. As a result, the combined model exhibits superior performance and is more resilient to variations in the number of nodes.
