By studying this distribution's moments, known as the multifractal spectrum, researchers can determine the unique characteristics of the semi-thermal phase. This approach is not limited to systems with multiple particles and can also be applied to systems with non-interacting particles. By implementing this method in various systems to assess their stability against the emergence of many-body localization, researchers can use it to classify these systems. For example, this method was used to study one-dimensional systems and revealed that certain modifications to these systems can shift the boundary between the ergodic and semi-thermal phases.

This paper addresses the problem of finding all items on a page that match a query as quickly as possible, a challenge in the field of human-computer interaction. Unlike traditional content-based search methods, which only reveal one result at a time and can be slow, this paper explores alternative approaches. Three of these strategies –- focusing on the most relevant items, spreading out across the page, and concentrating on distinct aspects of each result –- are examined, and an experiment was conducted to assess their effectiveness in finding multiple target items on a single web page under time constraints. It's found that a mix of these techniques and a simple adaptation of the best-known method lead to significant improvements in finding all target items efficiently.

The discovery of universal perturbations and instances that can deceive quantum classifiers has significant implications for quantum computing's future in machine learning. This advancement serves as a quantum equivalent of the well-known 'adversarial hypothesis,' providing valuable insights into designing robust quantum neural networks. Our research presents example inputs that universally fool quantum classifiers based on IBM's 5 and 7 quantum processor protocols, under specific measurement metrics. Additionally, we examined the tolerance of these models to noise and found that noise in certain forms can actually enhance their performance. Our findings contribute to the growing body of research exploring quantum machine learning and the development of quantum neural networks.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues in almost spherical areas and establish lower 
and upper bounds, with a focus on perturbations. Specifically, we demonstrate 
that these bounds are directly linked to the isoperimetric ratio of the domain 
and its first non-zero mean curvature, while also dependent on the average 
curvature. Furthermore, these results can be applied to various geometric and
non-geometric problems.

A established method for evaluating conformance in process analysis leverages alignments to assess and visualize deviations between model-expected and actual system-traced behavior. This paper extends alignments by combining three variants – prefix, infix, and postfix – to accommodate various temporal occurrences in single-trace conformance analysis, including instances that cannot be covered by prefix alignments. Infix and postfix alignments are developed to effectively combine and compare temporal occurrences in conformance verification, with a new example trace and alignment-based visualization illustrated in this study.

Accurate simulation of radio transmission in complex cellular networks requires detailed models of signal patterns, signal strength decline, and interference. Current proprietary tools fall short, leading researchers to develop faster and more precise alternative methods. A recent approach involves using convolutional neural networks to train models on proprietary data, generating synthetic signal patterns that closely match the original patterns. By leveraging this technique, researchers can bypass the need for proprietary data and create more efficient and precise transmission models. Studying the performance of these networks, researchers aim to understand how they generalize when applied to unseen areas and how they can be updated to optimize accuracy.

A formal semantics for temporal planning has been established and used as the basis for a verification tool, designed to ensure that a planned timeline adheres to specified temporal requirements. The tool leverages Isabelle/HOL, an interactive higher-order logic proof system, to define and validate the timeline and underlying temporal logic. The verification process within this framework involves translating high-level temporal requirements into a formal language and subsequently proving their validity through Isabelle/HOL's automated and interactive proof tools. The tool's effectiveness is demonstrated by successfully verifying simple temporal plans.

Power system expansion models, which are used widely, yet lack transparency, 
making it difficult to make informed decisions after running simulations. The 
predictive tools rely on complex power system models that use optimized or 
heuristical approaches with hidden parameters and lose their predictive 
accuracy over time due to model simplifications and approximations. In order 
to gauge a power system simulation model's predictive capability, our study 
puts forth a set of specific criteria for evaluation. The analysis of these 
criteria reveals that long-term power system expansion models are inherently 
susceptible to certain types of errors and biases, which ultimately impact 
the predictions made by power system simulation models. The conclusion drawn 
is that power system simulation models should be viewed as black-boxes with 
established rules and limitations. The understanding of these rules and 
limitations can lead to their improved effectiveness and help address models' 
shortcomings, which in turn, results in more precise and reliable power system 
predictions.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson-Vlasov-Vlasov and the Vlasov-Newton-Vlasov systems within confined areas with various boundary conditions, maintaining positivity for key variables and a specified symmetry in velocities.

When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely related requests from end-users, making it challenging to pinpoint relevant parts of the code (known as "search keywords") necessary to fulfill each request. Unfortunately, developers often struggle to determine these keywords, as users fail to provide them or submit inadequate search terms. To address this issue, our study proposes an innovative information retrieval-based approach ("STRICT") that aims to automatically extract relevant search keywords from user requests, drawing on existing concept location techniques. By treating search keywords as a record of the concepts users have previously identified during similar requests, our approach relies on the analysis of multiple related requests and their corresponding search terms. Given that search keywords vary greatly across different programming languages, our technique incorporates a query transformation stage that adapts initial requests to identify relevant code elements based on the specific language being used. Our approach ("STRICT") acts as a problem-solving assistant, taking an initial user request and applying it to find relevant search keywords within a given system, ultimately circling back to improve the original request and iteratively refine the identification of relevant search keywords until it meets predefined quality standards. During our experiments, our approach ("STRICT") demonstrated superior performance relative to baseline techniques, successfully extracting relevant search keywords from 61.5% of requests.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels, which show exceptional sensitivity to ultrasonic waves. This discovery reveals that when subjected to these waves, certain colloid gels undergo significant structural changes, losing their rigidity and transforming into liquids with reduced viscosity. This effect is highly dependent on the intensity and frequency of the ultrasonic waves and the gels' inherent properties. Simulations suggest that this reaction involves the ultrasonic waves causing particles to temporarily break free from the network of connections that holds them in place. This phenomenon allows for the manipulation of gel properties, enabling the gels to be easily poured and then re-solidified with ultrasonic treatment. This breakthrough introduces a new area of research for exploring the interaction between mechanical forces and acoustic waves that influence the structure and flow of materials within colloids.

The Collatz Conjecture is a well-known hypothesis in the field of number theory. It asserts that when you initially start with any number greater than 1, you can create a specific sequence by repeating two operations (dividing by 3 and then rounding up, or doubling the number) such that the sequence eventually reaches 1. Although numerous experts have studied this problem for centuries, solving it remains an unresolved challenge that continues to attract the interest of many mathematicians.

To develop a more precise model for identifying the connection between a particular entity and a larger document containing technical information on science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, we are focusing on breaking down complex documents into smaller parts. This involves two key components: one that identifies the most crucial elements within each section and another that determines the overall significance of these elements to the entire document. By utilizing the annotations provided by domain experts, we are constructing a network where all entities are linked to their relevant categories, and we are using this information to learn which entities are connected to a particular document's classification. This approach would enable a classification model to not only rely on the overall context but also to focus on the most critical parts of a document when making a classification. As a initial step in this direction, we are exploring a different technique called ME-LINK, which involves identifying the entities within a document that are connected to relevant categories, and is trained using the existing annotations in a one-way approach.

To guarantee matching stability in two-sided markets with distinct choices, economists often employ complex mechanisms. This paper introduces a straightforward new approach that restricts agents' available options by integrating all prior interactions into a single, limited choice set before making a final matching decision. The proposed mechanism is based on a simple query process, where the central authority creates subsets of possible choices and asks agents to rank them. Based on the resulting rankings, the authority matches the agents. The paper demonstrates that a straightforward matching rule results in a stable platform when agents accurately report their preferences and demonstrates significant efficiency gains, especially in large markets, while showing resilience against strategic behavior and computational efficiency improvements. The introduction of this new mechanism is part of a larger theoretical investigation into the design of stable market mechanisms with a limited number of choices.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are
highly unreliable in assessing human quality and limit the variety of generated
summaries in pre-trained models. To overcome these shortcomings, a novel
evaluation metric, SummScore, is proposed, designed specifically to gauge the
quality of summarization models. This innovative metric uses a Cross-Encoder
to measure the performance of generated summaries by evaluating their relevance
to the original sources through both coherence and redundancy analysis. This
approach distinguishes SummScore from existing evaluation methods, making it
more sensitive to variations in summarization performance. To develop SummScore,
a comprehensive dataset of 113K annotated summaries is introduced, marking the
first time human quality assessments are directly applied to summarization.
By replacing traditional evaluation metrics with SummScore, a new state-of-the-art
performance is achieved on three diverse summarization tasks, indicating its
versatility and effectiveness. Further studies document the benefits of SummScore
in its robustness, cross-lingual adaptability, and ability to facilitate human-
model alignment in the field of summarization.

We investigate a class of functions on [0,1] that have a certain level of smoothness and are bounded, and propose a measurement procedure that involves taking a polynomial of a specific degree, d, across evenly spaced subintervals of length 1/d. The goal is to design this measurement procedure such that its statistics satisfy two conditions: the probability distribution of the measurements should be as even as possible; and the distance between the distribution obtained from this procedure and the original signal should not exceed a certain limit times the smoothness of the signal raised to a certain power. We establish that such a procedure exists, and for a particular type of signals, demonstrate that the resulting statistics can be distinct enough to allow for exact recovery of the signal from a small subset of measurements. Specifically, for signals that are twice differentiable, we show that a measurement procedure exists such that most signals can be recovered from as few as 2-d measurements. Furthermore, for signals that are n times differentiable, we show that a measurement procedure exists such that most signals can be recovered from as few as (n plus 0.5) times 2 to the power of n measurements.

The simultaneous use of LiDAR data and camera images in pose estimation and scene understanding has shown significant potential, but existing fusion methods are often limited by complex architectures, restrictive assumptions, or a lack of explanations. To tackle these issues, a new unified representation learning approach for LiDAR-cameras has been developed, one that leverages the spatial structure of BEV and the strength of 2D-3D alignment. This approach, called BEVFusion, uses a simple and efficient framework to capture the interrelationships between LiDAR data, camera images, and beam-ray objects in a unified format. By incorporating the weighted sum of BEV and 2D representations, BEVFusion seamlessly aligns LiDAR data and camera images in a pose-agnostic manner. As a result, the framework enables clear mapping between LiDAR data and camera images, and the implicit network can perform 2D-3D alignment without any additional components. To demonstrate its effectiveness, a new benchmark for LiDAR-camera fusion has been developed, and BEVFusion has achieved top results on both semantic segmentation and object detection. Moreover, the framework has shown superior adaptability when working with small datasets, and it requires minimal processing capabilities.

In 1941, the concept of thermal fluctuations was first introduced by Penzias and Ramasesh, and since then, the development of hydrodynamic turbulence theories has accelerated. Researchers have, however, struggled to quantify the effects of thermal disturbances on turbulence and vice versa. The recent discovery by Kuz'min and Yu in 2013, suggesting that thermal fluctuations induce the energy cascade in turbulence, has significantly altered the understanding of this phenomenon. The study of turbulence has thus shifted from a purely inertial framework to one that incorporates thermal disturbances. The authors of this study have built upon this new understanding, developing a model in that the thermal cascade and energy cascades in turbulence are intertwined. The breaking of parity and reflection symmetries by the magnetic and thermal flows has facilitated the creation of complex structures such as magneto-hydrodynamic turbulence and also induced the formation of such structures in the presence of special magnetic fields. The study of the effects of thermal disturbances on turbulence has led the authors to predict rare atmospheric phenomena, such as bright spots and striations, which have previously gone undocumented in scientific literature.

We have developed an accurate numerical approach to study how heat affects the refractive index of a liquid when it undergoes laser-induced excitation, leading to intricate diffraction patterns. By focusing on water and carbon disulfide, we've investigated the red and blue areas in experimental patterns caused by spatial phase fluctuations. Our results uncover underlying dynamics and provide insights into heat diffusion, refractive index change, and optical absorption within the liquid. Moreover, our approach can describe larger spatial patterns that arise due to specific optical phenomena, such as fission and fusion processes.

Extracting design discussions from shared designs can enhance design feedback and feedback quality by providing designers with relevant feedback to refine their work. Current approaches to design discussion extraction rely on machine learning models that are prone to inconsistencies in interpreting design elements and user feedback due to the subjective nature of human creativity. A significant limitation in this area is the lack of a stable extraction system that consistently applies the same feedback selection for identical design elements across all users. To create a more stable extraction system, we developed a conclusion stability metric and applied it to compare the consistency of human and machine-based design discussion extraction. A comprehensive user study evaluated the performance of our proposed approach, which demonstrated higher stability than existing methods with an average increase of 40% in conclusion stability. By addressing this issue, our proposed system offers designers more reliable feedback to facilitate their work.

We introduce a novel language, called HSTREAM, for expressing the flow of data streams and their accompanying time series, combining the advantages of relational queries and streaming reasoning. This framework enables the joining of streaming information with prior data and the simultaneous analysis of incoming data and historical records. In contrast to earlier techniques, HSTREAM allows for the seamless integration of streaming queries with data retention policies, thereby facilitating the efficient storage of near-real-time and long-term data in relational databases. This paper outlines HSTREAM and demonstrates its potential through a case study on smart grids, also presenting it as a prototype system.

In recent years, the concept of a single, unified stream has been developed into a formal framework, extending beyond individual values to encompass near-real-time collections of near-real-time items over a significant and expanding period. This long-term collection, known as HISTORY, is subject to evolving state transformations, based on streaming reasoning coupled with data retention policies. This integration of streaming and relational reasoning enables both real-time analysis and long-term strategic decision-making for complex systems. However, the challenge of joining this real-time data with its accompanying HISTORY is yet to be addressed, along with the issue of near-real-time data retention. The development of a prototype system based on this approach is also described.

The search for unconventional top and bottom partners at the LHC has primarily focused on scenarios where the production of these particles occurs alongside standard model bosons. In contrast, we have investigated the potential of a different mechanism, where a top or bottom partner is produced alone, under conditions where there's no precise alignment between the production of an underlying standard model particle. Specifically, we have analyzed the scenarios of a singly-produced top partner interacting with standard model gluons and a doubly-charged particle, as well as a singly-produced bottom partner interacting with standard model photons and a doubly-charged particle. By using a specific type of variable that reduces experimental uncertainties and distinguishes background processes, we have found that, in certain cases, it's feasible to discern partners emerging from both the standard model at 13 TeV but also at an eventual 27 TeV LHC.

A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models has shown significant progress, but these models struggle to incorporate knowledge base knowledge into translated queries. Building upon this achievement, we introduce an innovative copy mechanism for NMT models to address this limitation. By enabling the copy mechanism to select and repeat knowledge base phrases during translation, the associated gap between human-written and machine-generated SPARQL queries is effectively bridged. Notably, our research reveals that the choice of pre-trained models for translating individual words and copied knowledge base phrases is crucial and can lead to better query translation. By incorporating the copy mechanism, the accuracy of SPARQL translation is notably improved when utilizing both small and large knowledge bases in testing scenarios.

This study examines the impact of a venue's reputation on the quality of its publications, including the limitations of relying on citation counts as a measure of quality. By presenting a novel method of venue analysis that automates the process, the research showcases a comprehensive evaluation of various scientific domains. Ultimately, the outcomes shed light on the effectiveness of citation-based metrics in evaluating a venue's quality and highlight potential future advancements in this area.

As a crucial part in the deployment process of control systems based on artificial neural networks, validation of the network's prediction accuracy across various observations is essential. There has been a lack of standardization in the techniques used for this validation. In the realm of control, it's necessary to ensure that the network's predictions allow the controlled system to meet its performance objectives. In this paper, a rigorous method of validating neural network predictions through the use of additional realistic scenarios beyond the initial training set is demonstrated. The proposed approach utilizes a long short-term memory network to create a dynamic predictor that can generate multiple scenarios. The feasibility of this technique is demonstrated through a simulation study involving a neural network-based predictive controller for a continuous stirred-tank system.

This study enhances the existing fuzzy fuzzy partition (FFP) framework in using Gaussian membership functions to facilitate clustering in cases of complex data sets with significant overlap regions. In doing so, a novel generation function is introduced that accounts for the fuzzy nature of both the group labels and the resulting clusters, all while maintaining the capability for distinct, non-overlapping groups if desired. Performance evaluation is achieved through several metrics; a distinctive characteristic of this approach is the utilization of vector-based learning in the fuzzy neural network (FNN) architecture to maintain the functionality for group label and cluster generation. Notably, the FNN is trained using vector-based learning to circumvent the limitations of traditional fuzzy clustering algorithms, all while generating multiple solution sets in response to different initial settings, in effect implementing multiple fuzzy clustering algorithms from a single framework.

The loss of original data due to degradation in video transmission can be overcome by utilizing video prediction techniques to estimate the missing information. However, existing video prediction models are hindered by two key limitations: the inability to accurately predict long-term data structures such as scene backgrounds and the failure to efficiently utilize historical frames when faced with temporal gaps. To address these shortcomings, a novel method called Patch Tracking-based Streaming Tensor Loop Completion has been developed for video data recovery. To enhance background prediction, a memory-augmented approach is used, allowing the model to retain information about last seen data structures. Furthermore, a patch tracking mechanism is designed to efficiently retrieve distant frames and bring them into the processing pipeline. By incorporating the Patch Tracking-based Streaming Tensor Loop Completion mechanism, the model can utilize a larger range of historical frames and tap into latent data structures, ultimately leading to the creation of a versatile and efficient VPC model for streaming video transmission recovery. Thorough experiments using the NTURCVS and Netflix datasets validate the effectiveness of this method.

It is demonstrated that with the exception of four exceptional cases, the Nichols algebras associated with irreducible finite reflection groups of rank two are directly isomorphic to the algebras derived from the root lattices of the corresponding finite Weyl groups, specifically A2, B2, C2, or D2.

Although wave turbulence theories have successfully predicted the long-term properties of oceanic surface wave turbulence, numerical simulations have revealed inconsistencies with the theories at short timescales. Specifically, intermediate-scale patterns have developed faster than the non-linear interaction rate would suggest. To resolve these discrepancies, researchers have created more accurate simulation models that incorporate the specific characteristics of the wave energy spectrum, which is based on a particular non-linear interaction theory by Zakharov and Kolmogorov. This modified model accurately replicates the spectrum of the wave turbulence as predicted by the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum. Furthermore, the new model has helped alleviate the simulation biases at short timescales.

In recent years, researchers have explored iterative approaches that incorporate graph filtering and normalization in deep learning frameworks, particularly for tasks related to identifying and quantifying key graph structures. Specifically, they have applied GraphSAGE and message passing neural networks to determine the maximum weight independent set and develop diverse node classification models. However, a notable insight from their research is that the iterative message passing process can be standardized by combining a graph normalization layer with an iterative message passing component. Under this condition, different iterative approaches converge towards similar outcomes. Notably, the study discovered that the MWIS problem is solvable within the proposed framework, provided that the iterative process is initialized with a specific initialization strategy. Moreover, they have demonstrated that the proposed framework can be adapted to support additional iterative approaches, including the maximum independent set problem.

This research investigates the thermodynamic properties of electrically controlled graphene monolayer in the context of the classical Drude model. Our findings reveal that the heat capacity and thermal conductivity are greatly impacted by the modulation process, exhibiting divinity and an unusual temperature dependence characterized by a complex series of increasing and decreasing values. Notably, these thermodynamic properties appear to be highly sensitive to external influences and electrical stimulation, suggesting that graphene monolayer meets the conditions for a topological system.

The system CR Draconis, consisting of two magnetically active M-dwarf stars, has been studied using full-disk spectra at a 166 MHz radio frequency over a period of 39 years. In most years, significant low-frequency radio emission from the stars could be detected, which after subtracting any interstellar background, showed a substantial variability on timescales of days to years. Spectroscopic and imaging analyses revealed that the source of this low-frequency emission is likely to be thin atmospheric layers, approximately 1-10 km in height, produced near the stars' magnetic poles. Our observations suggest that strong bursts of radio emission, associated with a high field region, are likely to be a common occurrence in active M-dwarfs, such as in the system CR Dra, which exhibits characteristics of an inverted source, produced through the two-stream instability triggered by a strong magnetic field. However, the radio emission in systems such as in the case of IM Men, which exhibits a different variability characteristic, is likely to be powered by a coronal process, which involves a channel of plasma linking the stars.

Our cutting-model visualizer presents 3D avatars in a novel, semi-translucent manner by leveraging pre-existing animation frameworks to generate a framework for visualizing the underlying 3D structure. This enables users to grasp the composition and movement of a character more easily. Our tool accommodates automatic characterization of nearly any animated character without necessitating re-animation. It can be accessed through a web interface at https://animeavatars.com.

There's a long-standing view that how humans and machines process visual information differ significantly.  While machines rely on precise, rule-based approaches, human vision is thought to be more flexible and influenced by various factors, including past experiences and higher-level cognitive functions.  To compare their performance under challenging conditions, a comprehensive set of severe image transformations has been created, along with a large, diverse image dataset.  Through comprehensive experiments involving both machine-based and human-based evaluations, distinct patterns of performance were observed, further validating the notion that machines and humans process visual information in notably different ways when faced with complex stimuli.

The Askey-Wilson matrix properties are used to show that a certain 3D version of the Chern-Simons theory based on a Lie algebra, when quantized using quantum group principles, results in a spectrum that can be expressed in terms of the polynomial coefficients of the 3-j symbol. Additionally, this connects the theory to the reduction of the full Hilbert space of the Chern-Simons theory in this specific Lie algebra context, leading to an infinite sequence of subspaces that are invariant to the quantum group action, corresponding to the eigenvectors associated with these invariant subspaces, which are expected to be a complete description of the theory's Hilbert space at the quantum level.

Our study involves a comprehensive analysis of two uniquely constructed 2D lattice structures composed of weakly interconnected trimer clusters, specifically the triangular and Kagome lattices on the cluster renormalization group's preferred trajectory. We utilize the cluster quantum Monte Carlo method to determine the ground state properties of these systems and their thermal evolution. We discovered that the Kagome lattice cluster quantum spin system exhibits a significant signature of antiferromagnetic long-range order at zero temperature, strongly suggested by a finite specific heat at the critical temperature. Conversely, the triangular lattice cluster quantum spin system exhibits a more complex behavior, exhibiting a disordered phase that persists at finite temperatures with a non-zero specific heat. These findings are supported by a cluster renormalization group framework, demonstrating that the systems' continuous quantum order parameter is integrally linked to the thermal expansion of the system. Furthermore, our research explores the thermal behavior of coupled cluster spin chains and the emergence of spin liquid phases.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited a "zero-shot" capability to execute various tasks by utilizing user-provided prompts. Nonetheless, their performance is still contingent on the efficacy of the devised prompt. To harness the potential of pre-trained models as versatile AI workhorses, developing a robust, zero-shot learning system is crucial. This paper introduces a novel framework for deriving a unified model that excels on multiple tasks. First, we assemble a comprehensive dataset comprised of task descriptions and corresponding prompts from cross-lingual language models, thereby creating a versatile dataset benchmark. Next, we design a prompt assembly pipeline to create a prompt ensemble, which is then fed into the pre-trained model to facilitate seamless task execution. Our research utilizes a GPT-3 model to evaluate this concept on three learning paradigms: few-shot learning, pseudo-labeling, and self-training, yielding impressive results that outperform the current state-of-the-art across multiple datasets and paradigm combinations.

In depth research into two NMSSM models that undergo a high temperature electroweak phase transition has been conducted, with a particular focus on those that exhibit $Z_3$ invariant properties. The study shows that in these models with correct electroweak chemistry and with neutrinos that are purely degenerate, a strong first order phase transition occurs, with predictions that can be both confirmed or contradicted by observations at the LHC and in dark matter investigation experiments. The predictions suggest a stronger signal for these models compared to the single NMSSM model with a much weaker LHC constraint. The study also shows that these models with correct electroweak chemistry result in significant tensor and vector contributions to the gravitational wave production, with a higher dominant role compared to other models, including the single NMSSM model and the two NMSSM models without $Z_3$ invariance. The investigation of these models against current LHC data and in dark matter investigation experiments, with respect to the LHC and in dark matter investigation experiments, also presents a promising opportunity to detect these gravitational waves.

We designed a statistical tool to assess the reliability of redshift measurements from millimeter and submillimeter waves with uncertain values. The tool evaluates the robustness of redshift estimates based on the differences between their values and those of adjacent pixels, with the goal of distinguishing between genuine and spurious signals. The sensitivity of this instrument varies as a function of the peak's width and the number of channels used. Employing this technique, we analyzed 101 interstellar molecules with multiple-channel data from the ALMA, APEX, and NOEMA telescopes, yielding 22 robust redshifts and 79 uncertain ones. Furthermore, we examined 64 interstellar molecules with a single channel and found 32 spurious signals and 32 uncertain ones. While this technique is not foolproof, as it failed to identify all robust signals and incorrectly classified some as such, it has proven effective in our experiments by identifying all robust signals from multi-channel data and the majority of robust signals from single-channel data.

This study is focused on the specific properties of certain quantum magnets.  We model a particular antiferromagnetic, which originates from $d$-waves N\'eel instability on a two-dimensional triangular lattice and features $S=1/2$ Heisenberg exchange interactions.  By performing large-scale Monte Carlo simulations, we have discovered the phase diagram, which includes the N\'eel and a $Z_3$ symmetry broken states, as well as a topologically liquid phase with four-fold symmetry.  This research identifies the dynamic signature of these three phases, specifically N\'eel order with $d$-wave spin excitations, $Z_3$ order with triangle spin excitations, and liquid behavior with certain unique characteristics, such as uniform and anisotropic spin excitations, which could also apply to other similar systems.

If we extend the unitary $SU(3)$ group beyond its fundamental representation, we observe that various phase transitions in a pure $SU(3)$ gauge theory occur at non-trivial critical points of the effective 2D $SU(2)$ magnetic flux lattice model. This is surprising since these transitions involve confinement, yet 2D does not confine. Moreover, our findings show that confinement arises in $SU(3)$ gauge theories at large distances due to the dynamics of magnetic vortices, which are analogous to monopoles, and the complex structure formed by them in different charge domains. This understanding leads us to deduce that the deconfinement-hadronization transition shifts significantly as we change the group representation used to extend $SU(3)$, which complicates the study of QCD phases.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a simple body-centered cubic (bcc) structure typical of many Al transition metal alloys and is unique among transition metal antiferromagnets with a high Curie temperature, featuring a small atomic moment and being highly magnetic resistant. To uncover the magnetic arrangement within the material, which was found to be of type I (magnetization directions meeting at four-valued nodes), researchers used neutron diffraction and electronic structure calculations using first-principles methods. These calculations, based on density-functional theory, allowed for the simulation of various magnetic arrangements and magnetic interaction strengths between adjacent Cr atoms. The findings suggest that interaction strength between nearest neighbor atoms dominates and can be approximated as being isotropic. The magnetic arrangement, which was confirmed through total energy analysis, is stabilized by a magnetic interaction of significant magnitude. The findings will serve as a foundation for further basic and applied studies aimed at developing this material into a thermally stable antiferromagnet within the field of spintronics.

A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, has been proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in kinetic theory. By integrating relaxation-time approximation and an anisotropic collision operator, the $
u$-model effectively captures the unique characteristics of rarefied gas dynamics influenced by the intermolecular potential. Analytical and numerical analyses of the model have been conducted for an equilibrium distribution function with velocity-dependent collision frequency. Specifically, solutions for the stationary Planar Couette problem have been obtained, and they depend on the particular potential used in Boltzmann's collision operator, indicating that the $
u$-model is a reliable tool for rarefied gas simulations. Furthermore, this model has been compared to the maximum entropy model, a different kinetic model, and it has been observed that both models' predictions converge as the Knudsen number tends towards a certain limit.

We evaluate the capabilities of a groundbreaking semantic parser known as the Naturalized Semantic Parser, developed by Marneffe et al. (2022), using a minimal dataset. This parser employs mBERT along with annotations derived heuristically from Prolog facts to represent logical forms of text. Testing was conducted on the HTLP dataset without utilizing the dataset's pre-annotated logical forms for training. Despite this constraint, the parser achieved a remarkable performance, surpassing previous parsers based on mBERT. Furthermore, the parser demonstrated an equivalent performance to a leading model, ARQM, which underwent extensive RoBERTa-based fine-tuning on the full HTLP dataset paired with Prolog facts. Subsequent enhancements to the parser included the incorporation of simple predicates and a text simplification preprocessing step, allowing the parser to match or exceed human performance on the dataset. Our results indicate that Naturalized Semantic Parsing can be effectively achieved using a very minimal amount of dataset annotations, transformed into Prolog facts reflecting the parser's target logic. This achievement holds significant potential for expanding the scope of NLP research to the practical domain of law, as well as accelerating the development of scalable, minimal-data semantic parsers.

Researchers are working on a future Electron-Ion Collider, where high-energy electrons will interact with high-energy ions at Brookhaven National Laboratory. The EIC will enable precise measurements of quark and gluon behavior by creating small regions of high energy density. Two collider detectors will closely study the interaction of electrons and ions, resulting in the creation of charged particles, which will be tracked in a detector ring. The development of a forward silicon tracker is underway in the EIC program. In this paper, we describe the design requirements, technical constraints, and technological considerations of a forward silicon tracker, then present two innovative technologies in development: a planar sensor with a very low microbarrel geometry, and nano mesa pixel sensors. The design constraints of a forward tracker, incorporating technology advancements and key features, are discussed, then the design of two sensor concepts is outlined, including description of the design process and component simulations. The potential performance of these sensor designs is explored through full simulations of the forward region.

A new ground-breaking discovery in the scientific literature details the identification of a newly discovered supermassive linearly growing black hole located at a massive distance from our Solar system. Specifically, researchers track how slowly but constantly a star at the center of this system moves toward a massive center, indicating that it is growing into a massive center powered by a steady process, not an explosion. Although these powerful emitters of light and heat are rarely observed in low-power centers, a close examination of a specific star's light shows that its brightness varies in a unique pattern, indicating either an explosion or a sudden mass drop occurring near a massive center. A comparison of these variations in light to predictions shows that either an explosion or a sudden mass drop occurred in this system, suggesting that either an explosion or a sudden mass drop can happen in low-power centers, indicating more research is needed.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars other than the most intense, chemically altered stars has long been supported by theoretical models, although there is still no concrete evidence for them. A key indicator of magnetic fields in stars is the positive radial field gradient, particularly in G-type main sequence stars. The detection of a magnetic field in the star HD58260 was significant in the past, and our analysis of new polarimetric data for this region also reveals strong evidence for magnetic fields, yielding a magnetic field map with an inconsistent slope of approximately $-6.0\pm 1.8 \,gcm^{-3}$ over a distance of approximately $0.20\pm 0.04\,R_{\odot}$. The characteristics of HD58260, such as its age, as well as the type and intensity of its magnetic field, correspond to those of stars with the ZDI magnetic field hypothesis, and our findings support this idea, showing agreement with this model. The findings of this research provide strong evidence of magnetic fields in magnetic field middle-class stars, as well as supporting the concept of a magnetic field sequence. The discovery of magnetic fields in magnetic field stars offers a vital opportunity to study their magnetic field structure, as a study of HD58260 has shown. The research points to an expected, chemically altered magnetic field structure, as determined by the ZDI magnetic field hypothesis, as well as the need for it. The search for magnetic fields in the star HD

A new representation of the Dunkl intertwining operator in one dimension in terms of a free boson field is developed, establishing a connection between the classical and quantum groups for the symmetric group via an application of the Fock space in two variables. This embedding also yields an explicit form of the local zeta function associated with the Hankel function.

Using ALMA's H30$\alpha$ line emission observations of the metal-poor galaxy NGC 5253, we have determined the rates of star formation in its molecular gas. Firstly, we used H30$\alpha$ to create a star formation rate (SFR) map, and compared it with a similar map generated from CO(1-0) emission, and also with a map generated from 1.4 GHz continuum radiation, all of which were corrected for extinction. Our results show that the SFR calculated from H30$\alpha$ is about 0.11 $M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, the SFR calculated from CO(1-0) is about 0.07 $M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, and the SFR calculated from 1.4 GHz continuum radiation is about 0.09 $M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$. When normalising these values to the total gas mass, we found the star formation efficiency (SFE) to be about $3 \times 10^{-3} \textrm{yr}^{-1}$, and noticed a significant gradient in the SFR and SFE in NGC 5253 with a slope 1.8, indicating higher formation rates at higher metallicities. Our observation of the high SFR and SFE in NGC 5253 aligns with the galactic metallicity trend. Additionally, by using H30$\alpha

We demonstrate that continuous orbit equivalence between virtually cyclic group actions on compact metric spaces results in orbit equivalence, using a mixture of established and newly formulated principles.

The operators of mathematical finance and data analysis, such as integration and expectation, have been generalized for functions that map a set of weakly distributed random variables to a Polish space. These generalized operators help to extend key results like the law of iterated expectations and Fubini's theorem to functions of random variables. Although initial work focused on parametric models, there has been a lack of research in nonparametric models until recently. Recent studies have established the law of iterated expectations and Fubini's transformation in a nonparametric setting, and we have built upon this by providing a novel, nonparametric estimation technique for the conditional expectation operator in a class of empirical processes. These techniques enable the consistent estimation of the conditional expectation without any prior distributional assumptions and have been successfully tested on various examples, including models with and without smoothness conditions.

Designing an observer to accurately track the dynamic evolution of an SIR model, which simulates the spread of a disease or virus, and understands the need for a suitable state observer in epidemiology. Although the SIR model has been extensively studied in various contexts, few have delved into the task of constructing an observer for this model. In this work, a suitable state observer is constructed for the SIR model using a specific control input, and an input signal is chosen to enable the tracking of the model's dynamic states by leveraging the output measurements. A stability analysis is also performed to ensure the tracking error remains within acceptable bounds over an infinite timeframe under a specifically selected input signal. Moreover, a numerical example is provided to illustrate the efficacy of the designed observer in practical scenarios.

Knowledge graph completion techniques aim to predict missing links by filling in an incomplete graph. Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) which incorporate time-based information, pose a challenge to conventional static models used for knowledge graph completion. Research has shown temporal models to be effective, but these methods demand significant memory and processing power, making them less suitable for large-scale TKGs. In contrast, static models can take full advantage of hardware resources but tend to perform poorly on TKGs. A novel approach has been developed, which utilizes static models for link prediction on TKGs by leveraging an edge-based temporal decomposition technique to separate and analyze individual relations. This method results in substantial performance gains for systems with limited resources, while also allowing for the efficient use of static models on TKGs. The method does not depend on any specific architecture or process, making it adaptable to a wide range of models. The proposed approach can be applied in combination with existing temporal models to fine-tune and speed up model training and prediction. Evaluations on multiple real-world TKGs demonstrate the method's capability to outperform static models and several temporal models in terms of link prediction accuracy and resource efficiency.

Research on ultrashort pulse generation in Kerr-lens mode-locking oscillators is gaining momentum, with further study necessary to fulfill their predicted potential. Our investigation contributes to this effort by providing a comprehensive analysis of their pulse-generation capabilities. Our approach involves critically evaluating the critical role played by the cavity's geometrical constraints, specifically beam expansion and contraction, within these oscillators. By incorporating experimental data from three diverse oscillator configurations, our research expands beyond theoretical understanding and bridges the gap between design considerations and performance outcomes.

A trend in modern machine learning research involves optimizing model training for diverse computational capabilities. This paper explores online federated learning for a nonlinear regression task via a new biobjective approach, distinguishing between collaborative learning speed and participant computation costs. Initially, the problem was tackled using a parallel trust region gradient descent algorithm under a fixed step size. However, due to asynchronous communications and variable step sizes, performance guarantees were lacking. The research resolves this issue by developing a dynamic step size strategy tied to learning speed objectives, resulting in stochastic optimization of the two objectives. The theoretical analysis yields a linear convergence rate under general noise conditions, supplemented by empirical evidence from real-world scenarios.

To optimize the absorption of solar radiation in thin silicon films, a photonic band gap back reflector is employed. By employing this setup, it's been demonstrated that a 10nm silicon layer can achieve the same absorption as a thicker layer (200nm) without the PBG mirror. Notably, even ultra-thin silicon layers can still provide high absorption rates (>90%) with the PBG mirror in place. This configuration also allows for the distinct spectral segmentation of the incoming solar radiation, further contributing to the efficient energy conversion process.

For a set of positive reals let's define $\mathscr{E}$ as the collection of sequences of positive reals that, when raised to successive powers, satisfy specific growth restrictions relative to another sequence in the set. This paper investigates functions defined on certain domains of the complex plane and, using $\mathscr{E}$, classifies them according to their behavior with respect to a complex variable changing at an exponential rate. In turn, these classifications reveal specific types of functions and generate a corresponding hierarchy of solutions to an exponential equation based on a positive function defined on the positives reals. Additionally, the equation's solutions can also be parameterized by sequences in $\mathscr{E}$, thereby expanding the scope of classification.

Building on the concept of coverings and high-dimensional extensions, we create novel techniques to derive new extenders in this field. A key discovery we make is that given certain conditions, the number of dimensions in a high-dimensional extension is directly related to the log of the size of its underlying domain. This connection allows us to harness results from additive combinatorics, specifically from the investigation of progressions in subgroups of finite groups, to create new high-dimensional extenders. Notably, our construction leads to the development of the first high-dimensional extenders that cannot be categorized as bounded-distance extenders or atomic expanders, thereby enriching the framework introduced by Impagliazzo and Wagner.

Researchers investigated the magnetic properties of the cleavage-oriented, centered honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO3 through comprehensive studies using magnetization, DC and AC susceptibility measurements, and detailed refinement of the crystallographic parameters.  This research found that the long-range magnetic order below 3.4 K is disrupted by significant disorder within the crystal structure, which is consistent at temperatures above 2 K.  Following a model that accounts for weak, non-uniform spin interactions, researchers were able to demonstrate that the observed magnetic behavior is accurately explained, even considering a weak, easy axis that aligns with the c-axis.  Furthermore, the temperature-dependent magnetic specific heat showed no distinct transitions, further indicating a two-dimensional magnetic phenotype.

Graph embeddings have gained significant attention for improving machine learning tasks on graph-based data. While most existing methods focus on learning over complex networks with abundant information, the case for sparse networks still presents significant challenges. Predicting links in such networks is crucial as it enables resource allocation in power grids, social connections in mobile communities, and medical relationships between organs. Motivated by the need to address these problems, our research introduces a new method, called SSNE, for creating node representations in sparse networks. By incorporating a key mechanism into a shared neural network framework, SSNE has the ability to handle the different characteristics of sparse networks. The performance of SSNE has been tested on various networks and shows remarkable improvements, producing Adam Adam results with reduced Adam loss rates, comparable to or surpassing state-of-the-art approaches.

A traditional silicon chip manufacturing process is modified to create a specialized cell for holding a thin layer of alkali metals, which have optical and magnetic properties due to their energy levels near the surface. The silicon chip's lower recessed area is filled with the vapor of the chosen metal, while the upper surface remains clean and conducts light from a nearby electrode to excite the vapor. The thickness of the vapor layer is precisely controlled by adjusting the pressure in the chip's closed system and can be monitored using a sensor. The chip's design allows for easy adjustment of the vapor layer height by heating the chip or changing the pressure, without the need for further fabrication. The manufacturer can select specific characteristics by altering the lower part of the chip to have specific reactions with the vapor, such as trapping specific energy levels, or having certain chemical properties that can adapt to different vapor conditions. Two designs have been created: a basic low-cost chip with a basic shape and a more advanced version with a more controlled light field. The more advanced version uses a specific chip feature to create a light field that can be adjusted by moving a nearby electrode to excite the vapor.

We compare the performance of various nonlinear Schrödinger models in predicting nonlinear distortion in dual-polarization transceivers, using a range of formats, including popular Lyapunov-based models and a more recent ergodic model, which we found to be particularly effective in this context.

A long-standing issue in satellite-based wildfire imaging has been addressed by a novel, high-performance technique that integrates near-infrared and visible images to produce high-quality visible images. This new approach, known as FIRe-GAN, is an efficient and powerful method that generates superior visible images from combined near-infrared and visible images. Comprehensive evaluations of FIRe-GAN were conducted using a substantial dataset of 15 wildfires in Canada, Spain, and the United States. These studies have yielded outstanding results, demonstrating the superior quality of the proposed technique. It is available for open access at https://github.com/cemkiyani/FIRe-GAN.

Early detection and treatment of depression is crucial, especially when children and adolescents are concerned, as it helps prevent serious complications and facilitates a quicker recovery process.  While mental health institutions provide essential services for identifying and treating depression, a notable lack still exists, partly due to the high demand for such facilities.  The proliferation of the internet and associated social media have significantly altered the way people live and interact, transforming them into an accessible means to access various services and connecting individuals with one another.  The aim of our study is to explore the possibilities of diagnosing and treating depression by collecting a dataset of social media posts relating to depression and training a predictive model to identify depression-related content.  The dataset was compiled by gathering 7,956 posts from 13 distinct depression-related sub-forums on the Chinese online forum, "Baidu", and divided into two categories: training data (75% - 5,976 records) and testing data (25% - 2,980 records).  Two machine learning algorithms were applied to the dataset: one natural language model, the character decomposition algorithm (CDA), and another, the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), both of which demonstrated substantial accuracy in predicting depression-related content.  The accuracy rates for the two algorithms were 70% and 65%, respectively.  By leveraging social media, individuals can gain access to depression diagnosis and treatment, ultimately promoting public awareness and understanding of this common mental condition.

We've developed a stochastic model that uses random compartment techniques to simulate the dynamics of COVID-19 infections in a general population. The model considers factors like demographics, proximity, hygiene practices, and severity of disease outcomes. It also assumes a non-uniform population with different exposure levels and risk of death from the virus. The model's core consists of three primary components: (i) a stochastic routine that creates a demographic population with the specified exposure and mortality characteristics, (ii) a compartment-based infection dynamics model that includes isolation, and (iii) a simulation routine that applies random stress events such as those simulated by Gompertzian growth to the model. These events can trigger larger outbreaks, leading to more severe cases and higher mortality rates. The model uses past data on US mortality rates to simulate scenarios, calculating measures like the cumulative percentage of the population that have died from the virus and average individual infection duration over time. It's shown that the model accurately predicts future mortality rates across different demographic groups when adjustments are made to the model parameters. This includes better performance than naive models that predict future outcomes based only on past trends.

The ISGMR and a $K = 0$ component of the ISGQR in nuclei with shell closures are accessed through $(e, e')$ scattering and studied using a computer simulation that includes the interaction of two important residual forces: one that affects the isoscalar monopole and quadrupole resonances. The resonance strength and the narrow width of the ISGMR in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si are used to demonstrate that this interaction of resonances significantly impacts measurements, resulting in a more accurate explanation of the data if this interaction is considered. The effect of this interaction is also found to have a noticeable influence on the width of the ISGMR in $^{28}$Si. The results of this simulation are then discussed in relation to theoretical calculations using the quasiparticle random-phase approximation (QRPA) and explore the significance of these results in understanding the interaction of forces that affect the structure of nuclei with shell closures.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of systems governed by Coulomb's law of friction is conducted. The research focuses on a one-dimensional motion of an object subjected to forces and with access to a velocity measurement, as well as a input force that can be adjusted based on that measurement. The adjustment of the input force is intended to enable smooth motion by avoiding the violent stick-slip cycles that occur when the motion is not controlled. Unpredictable force perturbations with a wide range of magnitudes are considered to mimic real-world systemic disturbances. A mathematical model representing this system is analyzed, and its properties are assessed to determine if it can actually avoid the stick-slip cycles. The adjustment of the input force is specifically designed to mimic either integral or proportional control mechanisms. When the adjustment is done in an integral fashion, a mathematical analysis shows that the system can actually avoid the stick-slip cycles, but this avoidance comes with the condition that a violent violent velocity change will always follow a slip phase. However, when the adjustment is done in a proportional fashion, a similar analysis shows that the system can actually get stuck in an infinite cycle of stick-slip alternations, and a similar analysis holds for a more advanced model that includes the effects of acceleration.

In the realm of quantitative finance, an often underexplored task called
no Claim Bonus (CB) forecasting has gained increasing attention from researchers
and practitioners. CB forecasting involves developing a system, known as a
predictive model, that accurately anticipates how future insurance premiums
will be impacted based on current conditions. This model then determines the
 optimal CB levels to install, which not only reduce installation costs but also
account for fluctuations in premiums due to various risk factors. Although
research on CB forecasting has progressed, there are still significant hurdles
to be overcome. Until now, most studies have focused on the'short' term, i.e.,
forecasting CB levels for relatively minor fluctuations in premiums. In
contrast, this study addresses the 'long' term, i.e., it explores ways to make
CB levels more dynamic and adaptable to significant fluctuations. A notable
contribution of this study is that it explores the application of reinforcement
learning (RL) in the context of CB forecasting. RL has the potential to enable
the development of optimal smart insurance policies that are dynamically adjusted
in response to various risk factors. In addition, this study integrates deep RL
in order to enable more precise predictions of CB levels in complex situations.
Furthermore, we use CB forecasting as a stepping stone to solve a related task,
known as optimal capital distribution (OCD), which has been extensively studied
in the field of quantitative finance. However, most studies on OCD have focused

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with next based on their past behaviors. Nonetheless, these models often struggle to account for users' distinct motivations, which can significantly impact their performance and user experience. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called latent user purpose modeling. By assuming that users have varying driving forces, we aim to identify and accommodate these factors. To achieve this goal, we developed three novel approaches that balance recommendation performance with the need to determine users' underlying motivations. Our approach uses the economic concept of elasticity to balance these objectives. Through comprehensive testing on real-world data, we demonstrated that our model surpasses the performance of widely-used recommender systems and effectively captures users' diverse purposes.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation, a special case of the general fourth Painlev\'e equation, can be formally obtained by unfolding the Fokas-Ablowitz equation, which itself is a limiting form of the general equation. The Fokas-Ablowitz equation arises when the Fuchsian singularities of a four-loop $t^{\frac{1}{4}}f(u)$ solution to the general equation blow up. The connection between the three equations can be understood through a process of unfolding. The process of unfolding, in turn, relates to a general equation that describes a folding of the solution space of a Fuchsian differential equation as part of a larger space. This relationship can be visualized in a manner analogous to a general symmetric unfolding of a Lagrangian connection. The resulting equation is a fourth-order ordinary differential equation.

Low-rank matrix recovery with an uneven data structure is an essential but underrepresented topic in the field of statistical matrix recovery. This study introduces a new model for restoring a matrix of rank one, characterized by an uneven distribution of data across groups, unequal variances, and distinct means. A multi-stage approach is presented to minimize the differences between the estimated matrix and its expected forms under the even distribution, with the bias terms suitably adjusted for group effects, variance, and rank. Different methods of estimating the low-rank matrix are developed, such as maximum likelihood, pseudo maximum likelihood, and least squares, in conjunction with specific estimation procedures for the matrix's positive semi-definite part and singular values. Various simulations illustrate the effectiveness of the methods and propose a new criterion for choosing the number of components in dimension reduction techniques like PCA when the population values are unknown. Finally, the method is successfully applied to a real-world data set in the field of astrophysics.

In carbon nanotubes, which are a form of carbon fullerenes, the atomic arrangement exhibits high levels of symmetry. Researchers initially hypothesized that this symmetry was essential for the formation of these nanoparticles. Contrary to this assumption, recent studies have shown that a different class of nanoparticles, called hypercarbon nanoclusters, can be synthesized without exhibiting any visible symmetry. This is made possible through the use of computational models, which allow for the exploration of a broader range of atomic configurations than is typically observed in three-dimensional structures. Furthermore, despite the absence of symmetry, these nanoclusters still maintain a unique inherent topological configuration that prevents them from taking on certain undesirable shapes. This topological structure is rooted in the connection relationships within the framework of the nanocluster and can be characterized by certain key intrinsic metrics, such as the Haesslin vector length and the Alexander-Polyak invariant. Additionally, the inherent topological arrangement of these nanoclusters gives rise to distinct properties, including specific patterns of oscillation and unique optical properties.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Invariance (LFI) ratio to compare
two observables that measure the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process in $B\to K\pi\ell^+\ell^-$
decays as recorded in different lepton flavour channels.
The LFI ratio enables us to assess whether data from various lepton flavours
comply with the hypothesis of no contribution from physics beyond the Standard Model.
In this context, we utilize experimental measurements from
Belle and BaBar collaborations to examine the LFI ratio, noting that
these values are susceptible to certain theoretical uncertainties as well as
systematic limitations periodically introduced by experimental findings.

In recent years, particularly in industry, the demand for large-scale distributed multi-channel systems with intricate structures has significantly increased, along with the need for effective network design and distributed algorithms to manage these systems efficiently. This research contributes to these efforts in two key ways: Firstly, it presents a novel decentralized design approach for linear multi-channel systems with an irregular network topology, which can be applied to various multiplexing techniques such as multi-user multiple-access and frequency division multiple-access, without necessitating a centralized controller. Secondly, it introduces a robust and decentralized management system that enables real-time resource management through efficient algorithms, translating to minimal end-to-end latency across the network. Notably, when the network topology is connected and the number of nodes is finite, our proposed management system even allows for the achievement of optimal performance in a wide range of critical metrics, such as overall power consumption, network throughput, and individual node utility. This research further explores the practical implications of these design and management approaches in real-world systems with complex structures.

This research explores the application of BERT features in categorizing COVID-19 into mild, severe, or critical forms. The approach combines two distinct models. The first, a binary classifier, differentiates between patients who have mild symptoms (vs. severe/exacerbated symptoms) using data from radiation therapists. The second, a three-class model, predicts patient outcomes based on information from both radiation therapists and critical care specialists. To enhance model performance, we treated the initial binary classifier as a two-cycle process, initially identifying critical cases, and then filtering out those cases for a three-class prediction. Our results demonstrate that the two-stage model produces accurate results for both critical care and multi-disciplinary teams.

Network science is a rapidly growing field with a wide range of applications across multiple disciplines, including physics, biology, computer science, sociology, epidemiology and epidemiology. This field has witnessed substantial growth over three decades, fueled by advancements in theoretical and computational methods. This surge in interest is driven by the increasing recognition of networks as a crucial tool for understanding various phenomena.

This comprehensive overview provides an accessible framework for navigating the intricate landscape of network science. It encompasses foundational aspects, cutting-edge techniques, and cutting-edge applications. This framework is designed to serve as a roadmap for both aspiring researchers and seasoned scientists, offering a thorough understanding of this multifaceted field and its vast potential for future breakthroughs.

We demonstrate how timescales and rate factors change in eco-evolutionary processes over extended periods.  Initially, variations in population sizes, mutation rates, and selection factors are independent of time.  As generations accumulate, variations in population sizes grow and become the dominant factor, eventually surpassing the impact of mutation rates.  Further generations ahead, the effects of mutation rates disappear completely, leaving variation solely dependent on changing effective population sizes, a consequence of the shifting dynamic.  We also examine the influence of body size on the rate of evolution, a factor that precludes significant eco-evolutionary changes in very large organisms, over their entire lifespan.  In contrast, smaller species remain susceptible to eco-evolutionary changes throughout their life cycles.  We provide empirical evidence from studies on the accelerated evolution of body size across various fish species.  Ultimately, the interconnectedness of timescales and rate factors holds the key to understanding the intricate processes of eco-evolutionary changes within ecosystems.

A study was conducted to understand how much exposure to adversarial examples affects self-supervised speech learning models. Researchers discovered that these models can be vulnerable to such examples, which are easily discovered through a simple approach. The outcome of the research has significant implications for these models, used in critical applications, as they can be compromised with relatively simple attacks and the results can also provide insight into their internal workings, as they tend to mislearn the subtle patterns that these models create internally. The study's findings are the first to show the effect of adversarial examples on these models and they suggest potential strategies for mitigating this issue in future work.

A growing number of decentralized finance (DeFi) applications on blockchain platforms have drawn the attention of academics and practitioners. The proliferation of open, permissionless blockchain technologies has enabled the creation of versatile applications, with a key component being the decentralized exchange (DEX). By assessing the potential risks and rewards, we develop a theoretical framework to analyze the adoption dynamics of DEXs. Specifically, as the user base grows, both benefits and costs tend to rise; however, at a point of market liquidity, costs shift towards a negative trend. Meanwhile, a novel DFX protocol has been designed to allow DEXs to transition from off-chain liquidation to on-chain trading, thereby addressing liquidation risks and thereby reducing the costs associated with it. By combining elements from stochastic diseases and the multi-armed bandit problem, we establish a complex dynamic where users decide between using DEXs and centralized exchanges. Given that DFX represents a more efficient trading platform, users have an incentive to collaborate to maximize their profits, resulting in a potential equilibrium where DFX becomes the dominant trading platform. Furthermore, users may experience an optimal strategy by applying the principle of the yield per effort, resulting in a boundary between efficient and inefficient liquidation, thereby providing guidance for operators of DEXs.

A new statistical approach, the 'E-value,' assesses how assumptions about missing data impact study conclusions. However, there's a gap between the E-value's theoretical promise and practical application, largely due to a lack of clear methodology for evaluating assumption validity regarding missing data. This study addresses this by creating a framework for choosing the most suitable assumption regarding missing data, using a Bayesian method. Among our key findings, the Bayesian method outperformed the conventional frequentist approach in testing for missing data, with significant results. This study also developed a method for determining the reliability of assumptions about missing data, using a Bayesian approach to "principle 1." Our method identified the validity of certain assumptions, shed light on the uncertainties surrounding others, and revealed the uncertainties associated with conclusions drawn under invalid assumptions. This study used data from two studies on mycobacterium tuberculosis, offering a step-by-step approach to the selection of assumptions about missing data and their evaluation, particularly for the treatment of control arms in clinical trials.

A multi-component Laurent extension of the quantum plane is a significant concept in non-commutative geometry. When expanded, it forms a new algebra that contains several copies of the quantum plane, along with higher-dimensional polynomial components. To study this expansion, we need to determine and classify its defining polynomials, which leads us to a comprehensive list of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-actions on the Laurent extension algebra. This classification allows us to understand how the quantum group operates within this non-commutative geometry and establishes a connection between the geometric structure and the associated algebraic properties. Moreover, our research reveals that most $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-actions on the Laurent extension algebra can be obtained through the quantum curl operator. This finding enables us to study the Casimir element and establish a link with quantum de Rham complex.

The integration of Cloud Computing drift services and intelligent communities of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, including Internet of Vehicles (IoV), is essential for providing efficient and safe transportation. Federated learning offers a promising approach for reconciling computation resource limitations and data security risks in multi-owner datasets. Nevertheless, security remains a top priority for IoV stakeholders. Considering the growing number of IoT devices with distinct characteristics, blockchain technology could develop into a decentralized key for sustaining secure and robust system environments. By merging blockchain and federated learning, researchers aim to construct robust machine learning systems resilient to adversarial attacks and ensure the reliable protection of sensitive information. This review encompasses existing blockchain-empowered federated learning literature, covering various aspects, including the motivation, framework, applications, challenges, and future prospects of BLE-based FL systems. This comprehensive study explores the unique challenges posed by the rapid advancement of BLE and FL, aiming to inspire novel solutions and pioneering innovations in the field.

The ALICE experiment measured $p$+$p$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV to develop a comprehensive understanding of charm and beauty quark production. This was achieved by analyzing data from the ALICE detector, which captured D-meson decay topologies in the central region. A differential analysis of non-prompt (bound in a quarkonium state) and prompt (not bound in a quarkonium state) D-meson production revealed significant information about parton fragmentation. A prompt D-meson cross-section assessment also provided insight into the underlying physics of charm quark collisions. Moreover, the study's results, expressed in terms of nuclear modification factor $F_{5.02}$, offered a glimpse into the effects of the hot and dense medium created in high-energy collisions. This observational study, characterized by a substantial cross-section, paved the way for a deeper analysis of charm and beauty quark collisions.

The growing influence of quantum computing has generated substantial interest in attaining long electron coherence times at cryogenic temperatures beneath 10 millikelvin in order to protect quantum bits using superconducting devices. Researchers are working on a cutting-edge experimental project situated at Fermilab, aiming to establish a large millikelvin system comprising superconducting qubits, superconducting flux pumps, and superconducting magnetometers to support quantum computing and novel quantum metrology initiatives. The project involves employing a cutting-edge $^4$He cryogenic magnetometer to Enflute a 4K stage to achieve temperatures of approximately 6 millikelvin using helium-3. The system will be reinforced by 6.7 Tesla boiting magnetic field provided by a DC superconducting magnet. The integration of this cutting-edge cryogenic control system combines heating mechnaism with electronic feedback will enable precise temperature and magnetic field modulation.
